documents/affordable-healthcare.md.text:
## Affordable Healthcare

Labour will make healthcare affordable again with three free doctor's visits, free prescriptions, free maternity scans and free cervical screening - all through one Medicard.

Labour's plan for affordable healthcare
- Free Doctor's Visits - three free GP visits a year for every New Zealander
- Free Prescriptions - the $5 fee removed from 1 July 2027
- Free Maternity Scans - everywhere in New Zealand from July 2028
- Free Cervical Screening - for ages 25 to 69, from 1 October 2027
- Family Doctor Loan Scheme - backing more local GPs to open and stay open

### Why it matters

Under Christopher Luxon, it's become harder and more expensive to see a doctor when you're sick.

1 in 6New Zealanders can't afford to visit their doctor

~$100Some GP visit fees are heading towards this

9 in 10New Zealanders won't pay Labour's targeted property tax

No one should have to choose between seeing a doctor and putting food on the table. Labour will build a health system that doesn't depend on what’s in your wallet.

### Labour's plan in detail

#### Free Doctor's Visits (Medicard)

Every New Zealander will get a new Medicard giving access to three free doctor's visits a year at their enrolled practice, funded by a simple, targeted tax on investment property profits.

Full policy details →

#### Free Prescriptions

From 1 July 2027, the $5 fee on prescriptions will be removed for every New Zealander entitled to public healthcare - no forms, no claiming money back.

Full policy details →

#### Free Maternity Scans

From July 2028, Labour will fund every scan a doctor, midwife or specialist refers a pregnant woman for, everywhere in New Zealand - no forms, no invoices.

Full policy details →

#### Free Cervical Screening

From 1 October 2027, cervical screening will be free for everyone aged 25 to 69, loaded automatically onto the Medicard and available at your local doctor or a community screening event.

Full policy details →

#### Family Doctor Loan Scheme

Labour will offer doctors interest-free loans for the first two years, of up to 90% of the cost of buying into a general practice (capped at $500,000), to encourage more owner-operated local clinics.

Full policy details →

A Labour government will also guarantee a job for every eligible graduate nurse, so our hospitals and clinics have the staff to deliver this care. See our full plan for good jobs.

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's Medicard?
The Medicard is a new card and app every New Zealander will receive, giving access to three free doctor's visits a year at their enrolled practice, free cervical screening (ages 25 to 69), and free maternity scans. Entitlements are loaded automatically.

What free healthcare will I get under Labour?
Under Labour, New Zealanders will get three free doctor's visits a year, free prescriptions, free maternity scans, and free cervical screening for those aged 25 to 69. Labour is also backing more local GP practices through the Family Doctor Loan Scheme.

How is Labour's healthcare plan funded?
Labour's healthcare policies are funded by a targeted 28% capital gains tax on profit from selling commercial or residential investment property, excluding the family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, businesses and inheritances. Every dollar raised is ring-fenced for health, and nine out of 10 New Zealanders will not pay the tax.

When do these healthcare changes start?
Free prescriptions and the Family Doctor Loan Scheme start from 1 July 2027. Free cervical screening starts from 1 October 2027. Free maternity scans start from July 2028. The Medicard's three free doctor's visits roll out alongside these changes.

Who is eligible for these entitlements?
The Medicard and its entitlements are available to every New Zealander entitled to public healthcare. Cervical screening is free for those aged 25 to 69. Maternity scans are free for anyone pregnant and eligible for publicly funded health services, with a referral from a GP, midwife or specialist.

Affordable, reliable healthcare is the foundation on which New Zealanders build their lives.

Better starts now.

documents/ai-for-new-zealand.md.title: AI in New Zealand’s Interests
documents/ai-for-new-zealand.md.text:
## AI in New Zealand's Interests

The challenge Our approach Next steps FAQs
A Labour Government will take an active role in shaping how AI develops in New Zealand, rather than leaving it to a handful of big technology companies to decide.

Our goals for AI
- Protect what matters. Protect people's rights, safety and privacy, protect creative work, and keep government decisions that affect people's lives accountable to people
- Unlock our potential. Help New Zealanders and businesses build the skills and capability to use AI productively and share in the benefits
- Lead on New Zealand's terms. Provide clear government leadership and oversight, and protect New Zealand's control over our data and our choices
- A new Office of AI within DPMC, and an online safety regulator
- A framework to recognise and pay creators when AI uses their work
- Rules requiring data centres to pay their own way on energy and water

AI is developing quickly and is already part of New Zealanders' daily lives. It offers huge opportunities to lift productivity, improve public services and help businesses compete. But we cannot leave it to a handful of big technology companies to decide how it shapes our future.

Change is happening. The question is how and who benefits. Now is the time to decide how AI works for New Zealand.

This action plan sets out that direction and the areas where we believe the government needs to act. AI will keep changing, so we will work with experts, businesses, iwi, educators, researchers, creators and communities to get the details right.

### The challenge

New Zealanders can see both the opportunities and risks of AI. Many are already using AI to save time and get more done, while also worrying about its wider effects.

The benefits will not be shared fairly - and the risks will not be managed in everyone’s interests - by chance. The Government has a responsibility to make sure AI works for everyone.

National is taking a light-touch approach that relies too much on existing law and decisions made by overseas technology companies. It has failed to provide a clear plan for addressing the issues New Zealanders are worried about, or ensure the benefits are shared beyond the biggest companies.

National is also planning to replace public service jobs with AI without answering basic questions about accountability or what it could cost taxpayers over time.

AI is not a one-off purchase. Agencies will have to pay ongoing licence and usage fees that could rise over time. If public services become too dependent on a small number of overseas technology companies, New Zealand could face significant and growing costs. There must also be safeguards to ensure AI is not making decisions about people's lives on its own.

We can't turn back the clock or press pause on AI, nor should we. But accepting that AI is changing how we do things does not mean that New Zealand has no say in how that change happens.

### Our approach

A Labour Government will:

- Provide leadership and coordination across government on the development, adoption and governance of AI
- Back investment and responsible adoption, helping New Zealand businesses to safely take advantage of AI
- Protect New Zealand's interests, including our data, creative work, iwi/Māori and public services
- Ensure AI is used safely and accountably, particularly in government decisions that affect people's lives
- Take a proportionate approach to regulation that addresses real risks without creating unnecessary barriers to innovation
- Work with Australia and other partners on shared standards and challenges

#### Five tests for AI decisions

Five tests will guide the decisions a Labour Government makes:

| Test |
| --- |
| 1. Are the gains shared beyond those who own the technology? |
| 2. Do people have a real say in how AI is used in their workplaces? |
| 3. Does a human still have meaningful oversight and accountability for government decisions that affect people's lives? |
| 4. Are AI companies using energy, water and land responsibly and carrying their fair share of the costs? |
| 5. Do New Zealanders retain control over our data, creative work and infrastructure? |

### Protect what matters

Trust is essential to the responsible use of AI. We will strengthen protections where AI can cause serious harm or erode trust.

A Labour Government will establish an online safety regulator. We will also expand an AI Expert Advisory Panel to bring together technical and legal experts, small business, unions, the arts, and iwi Māori, reporting directly to Ministers as the technology develops.

The group will advise the Government on emerging issues and help make sure we seize the opportunities from AI while managing the risks and protecting what matters to New Zealanders.

#### Creative work

Not everything produced in New Zealand is up for grabs. Writers, musicians, artists, journalists and other creators should retain meaningful control over how their work is used, and should be properly recognised and rewarded for its value.

We will develop a framework for the use of copyright material by AI, including how creators can control and be remunerated for the use of their work. We will work with creators, publishers, technology companies and others to get those settings and their enforcement right.

#### Safety and accountability

AI-enabled scams, deepfakes, non-consensual images and threats to children are growing.

We will identify gaps in New Zealand law and strengthen protections where needed, rather than only relying on technology companies to regulate themselves. These protections will include banning non-consensual deepfake pornography. We will also establish clear standards around the use of private information, such as health data.

AI can help people make better decisions, but it shouldn't make decisions about people's lives on its own. The National Government has changed the law to allow automated decision-making within MSD.

A Labour Government will establish clear expectations for human oversight and accountability in the public service, and review how existing privacy, consumer and employment protections apply to AI. When the government makes a decision affecting someone's access to a service, a person must remain accountable.

#### Infrastructure

AI needs land, energy, water and computing power. The impact on our environment and resources needs to be carefully managed.

A Labour Government will set clear rules for large data centres so their growth does not leave households and businesses carrying the cost or put pressure on water and electricity supplies. We will require data centres to secure their own renewable energy supply, pay for their own connection costs, reduce electricity demand during peak stress periods, and use water efficiently.

Our approach is simple: the right-sized data centre in the right place, with the companies that benefit carrying their fair share of the cost.

### Unlock our potential

The gains from AI must reach beyond the companies that build it.

#### Work

AI will change how New Zealanders work. Done well, it can increase productivity and create new jobs. But that won't happen on its own.

We will work with businesses, educators, experts and unions on the skills people will need, and on making sure productivity gains show up in wages and conditions. We will back accessible training opportunities, including micro-credentials, so people stay in work in a world of AI, rather than be displaced by it.

AI should make working people more productive and open up new opportunities, not become an excuse to cut jobs and shift the benefits to those at the top.

#### Small business and communities

AI has the potential to help small businesses become more productive. Labour has already committed support for small businesses to adopt AI safely through the AI small business fund, an extension to the AI Advisory Pilot, and an increase to the Founder and Startup Support Programme.

We will build on that to make sure reliable information and guidance is easier to access.

#### Public services

AI has the potential to make public services faster and easier to access. For example, it can help cut down hospital paperwork so busy doctors and nurses have more time to look after patients. But it cannot be an excuse for cutting thousands of jobs.

We will use AI where it genuinely improves services while maintaining human oversight and accountability. We will also take steps to understand the full lifetime cost of adopting AI across the public service.

#### Education and digital equity

Community organisations, schools and other organisations should not be left to work out the risks and opportunities on their own.

A Labour Government will make sure there is clear and adequate support for schools to ensure AI can be used safely, for teachers and for students. Labour will enable an AI in Education team to support schools, teachers and students. We will bring guidance together, help organisations make informed choices, and monitor our success.

### Lead on our terms

AI crosses almost every part of government, but responsibility for responding is currently split across ministers and agencies.

#### Office of AI

We will establish an Office of AI within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC) to coordinate New Zealand's approach. The office will be established from existing resources, not a new layer of bureaucracy. Its role will include:

- Coordinating AI policy across government
- Developing proportionate standards for responsible AI use
- Developing a long-term plan for New Zealand's workforce with working people, employers, unions, and industry
- Setting expectations for government procurement
- Promoting consistency and transparency across the public service
- Identifying emerging risks and opportunities

A senior minister will be responsible for AI, and the whole-of-government programme of work will be published so New Zealanders can see what action is being taken.

#### Data sovereignty

This is a huge challenge. However, New Zealanders should have a say over how their data, and data collected here, is stored, governed and used.

We will look at how to strengthen New Zealand's control over its data rather than simply accepting the rules set by global technology companies. We will also work with iwi and hapū on how Māori data is collected, owned, governed and used.

#### Working with others

New Zealand cannot address every challenge created by AI alone. We will work closely with Australia to align standards and approaches where doing so benefits New Zealand. We will also work with Pacific countries on shared safety and security challenges.

### How we will move forward

This action plan sets the direction a Labour Government will take. Getting the detailed settings right will take time and proper consultation.

- Set the direction. We will take steps early to establish the Office of AI, appoint a lead minister, and publish a coordinated programme of work across government
- Listen and assess. We will work with those building, using and affected by AI to identify the most urgent risks and the biggest opportunities
- Act where the case is clear. We will move quickly in the areas where there is the greatest need, while taking time to get complex settings right
- Measure and adapt. We will use evidence and independent advice to monitor what is working and adapt where necessary

#### What success looks like

Success will not be judged by the number of strategies, agencies or regulations we create. It will mean:

- New Zealanders can trust that AI is being used safely, transparently and fairly
- Data centres pay their own way on energy and water without additional costs on households or businesses
- Government decisions that affect people's lives remain accountable to people
- Creators retain meaningful control over their work and its value
- People, small businesses, schools and communities can access and share in the benefits of AI
- New Zealand sets its own rules, rather than accepting rules set for us somewhere else
- AI helps Kiwis get ahead

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's AI policy?
The AI Action Plan sets out a framework for how government to actively shape how AI develops in New Zealand, built around three goals:
- Protecting what matters (people's rights, safety, privacy and creative work)
- Unlocking New Zealand's potential (helping people and businesses build the skills to use AI productively)
- Leading on New Zealand's terms (government leadership and control over New Zealand's data and choices)

What is the Office of AI?
A new body Labour will establish within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC) to coordinate New Zealand's approach to AI, established from existing resources rather than a new layer of bureaucracy. A senior minister will be responsible for AI, and the whole-of-government programme of work will be published. Its role will include:

- Coordinating AI policy across government
- Developing proportionate standards for responsible AI use
- Creating a long-term workforce plan
- Setting expectations for government procurement
- Identifying emerging risks and opportunities

How will Labour protect creators and copyright from AI?
We will work with creators, publishers and technology companies to develop a framework for the use of copyright material by AI, including how creators such as writers, musicians, artists and journalists can control and be remunerated for the use of their work.

How will Labour regulate AI-enabled harms, like deepfakes and scams?
Labour will establish an online safety regulator, identify gaps in New Zealand law, and strengthen protections where needed rather than relying only on technology companies to regulate themselves.

This includes banning non-consensual deepfake pornography and establishing clear standards around the use of private information, such as health data.

What rules will Labour apply to AI data centres in New Zealand?
We will set clear rules for large data centres so their growth does not leave households and businesses carrying the cost or put pressure on water and electricity supplies. Data centres will be required to secure their own renewable energy supply, pay for their own connection costs, reduce electricity demand during peak stress periods, and use water efficiently.

Will AI be allowed to make decisions about people's lives on its own?
No. Labour will establish clear expectations for human oversight and accountability in the public service, and review how existing privacy, consumer and employment protections apply to AI. When a government decision affects someone's access to a service, a person must remain accountable, not an automated system alone.

How will Labour support small businesses and working people to use AI?
Labour will work with businesses, educators, experts and unions on the skills people need, back accessible training including micro-credentials, and aim to ensure productivity gains from AI show up in wages and conditions rather than job losses alone.

What data sovereignty protections will Labour introduce?
Labour will look at how to strengthen New Zealand's control over its data, rather than simply accepting rules set by global technology companies, and will work with iwi and hapū on how Māori data is collected, owned, governed and used.

A Labour Government will make AI work for New Zealanders, not just the companies that build and own it.

Protect what matters. Unlock our potential. Lead on our terms.

documents/apprenticeshipboost.md.text:
## Expanding Apprenticeship Boost

Labour will support more tradies and young people into work and to gain a qualification, so they can earn more.

Key facts
- Employer payments extended from one year to two years at $500 a month, effective 1 July 2028
- $1,000 toolbox grant to help new apprentices cover the cost of getting started, including tools, kit, uniform, and course materials, available from 1 July 2027
- Eligibility expanded to five new trades - road construction, water and sanitary engineering, personal services, sales and marketing, and sports and recreation - from 1 July 2027
- Structured mentoring piloted from 1 July 2027 via Industry Skills Boards and providers, supporting both apprentices and employers, starting with those most in need
- Average cost of $56.5 million a year over four years, fully paid for

### Why is this important?

Too many New Zealanders feel their only option is to go overseas for work they can't find at home, and youth unemployment keeps climbing. It doesn't have to be this way.

Expanding Apprenticeship Boost helps more tradies and young people earn while they learn, building secure, well-paid careers right here at home.

Christopher Luxon's cuts, pauses and delays to major projects have cost the construction industry 20,000 jobs in three years. Building the homes, roads, schools and hospitals New Zealand needs means planning ahead, giving businesses certainty, and training the people who'll build them - and expanding Apprenticeship Boost is a practical step to make it happen.

Frequently asked questions
What will businesses get?
$500 a month to help cover the cost of taking on an apprentice and supporting their development.

What will apprentices get?
A $1,000 toolbox grant to cover the cost of getting started, plus mentoring and extra support to help them stay the course to full qualification.

Which trades are covered?
Any accredited apprenticeship programme, including five new areas - road construction, water and sanitary engineering, personal services, sales and marketing, and sports and recreation.

How much will it cost?
As more people benefit, the investment in Apprenticeship Boost will increase steadily over time, starting at $21 million in 2027/28, increasing to $71.5 million in 2030/31, averaging at around $56.5 million a year over four years.

When will it start?
New trade eligibility, the mentoring pilot and the $1,000 toolbox grant all begin 1 July 2027. The extension to two years of employer support starts 1 July 2028.

Backing tradies and young people to gain a qualification keeps our people and their skills here in New Zealand.

## Backing Māori Businesses

Labour will reinstate Progressive Procurement, with an initial target of 5% of government procurement contracts allocated to Māori businesses.

Key facts
- Progressive Procurement reinstated
- Initial target of 5% of government procurement contracts allocated to Māori businesses
- Approximately $900 million worth of contracts could be awarded to Māori businesses
- Based on the previous policy, which Labour says shows 5% is both deliverable and sustainable

### Reinstating Progressive Procurement

Māori businesses up and down the country have demonstrated that they can deliver. That's why Labour will reinstate our Progressive Procurement policy, because we know it works.

Like Labour's small business first policy, we will aim for an initial target of 5% of government procurement contracts to be allocated to Māori businesses.

Based on the previous policy, we know that 5% is both deliverable and sustainable.

This means that approximately $900 million worth of contracts could be awarded to Māori businesses, injecting much needed capital into businesses and supporting wider socio-economic growth. It's a win/win for everyone.

Read about Labour's Small Business Action Plan →

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's policy for backing Māori businesses?
Labour will reinstate its Progressive Procurement policy. Māori businesses up and down the country have demonstrated that they can deliver, and Labour knows the policy works.

What is the Progressive Procurement target?
Like Labour's general small business policy allocation, Labour will aim for an initial target of 5% of government procurement contracts to be allocated to Māori businesses.

How much could Māori businesses receive in government contracts?
Approximately $900 million worth of contracts could be awarded to Māori businesses, injecting much needed capital into businesses and supporting wider socio-economic growth.

Is a 5% target realistic?
Based on the previous policy, Labour knows that 5% is both deliverable and sustainable.

How does this relate to Labour's small business policies?
The 5% initial target mirrors the allocation in Labour's general small business policy. See Labour's Small Business First policy and Small Business Action Plan for more.

More Māori in business means more Māori in sustainable employment, growing the Māori economic asset base and lifting incomes for whānau.

Better starts now.

documents/banking-for-everyone.md.text:
## Banking for Everyone

More competition Backing Kiwi innovation What Labour will change Kiwibank stays Kiwi FAQs
Labour will open banking up to more competition, so Kiwis get better prices, better services and more choice.

Key facts
- Major banks required to give smaller competitors fair access to payment systems and banking information
- A new digital banking licence lets payments companies grow into digital banks
- Secure, 24/7 real-time payments for fintechs delivered by 2030
- Kiwibank remains 100% New Zealand-owned
- Government-verified ID option for switching providers, and clearer, more comparable insurance terms

New Zealanders and Kiwi businesses should be getting a better deal from their banks.

Almost everyone relies on a bank - to get paid, pay the bills, buy a home or get finance to grow a business.

But the big four hold around 85 to 90 percent of registered bank assets and their profits are high compared with banks overseas.

Labour will open banking up to more competition, so Kiwis get better prices, better services and more choice.

And we'll back innovative New Zealand financial businesses to grow, create jobs and compete with the big banks with new and better ways of doing things.

### More competition means a better deal

Banking in New Zealand is controlled by four big banks - ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac.

They play an important role in our economy. But their control of the market makes it harder for new competitors to break through. That matters because competition puts downward pressure on prices and improves services.

Small businesses feel it too and can often pay around 4.5 percentage points more in interest than big businesses.

The big banks are putting a smaller share of their lending into businesses while focusing more heavily on mortgages. That makes it harder for a good Kiwi business with a good idea to get the backing it needs to grow, employ more people and lift wages.

Labour wants banks competing harder for your business - and more businesses competing with the banks.

### Backing Kiwi innovation

Stronger competition doesn't have to mean waiting for another big bank to come along. It can come from smaller, innovative companies offering a service better or cheaper.

We've already seen it with international money transfers. Companies such as Wise have made it easier and cheaper to send money overseas and forced traditional banks to compete.

New Zealand has talented people building new financial technology here too. They could be developing cheaper payment services, smarter digital wallets, easier ways for businesses to get paid, or entirely new banking products.

We want those businesses starting here, growing here and creating good jobs here.

But too often they hit barriers that favour the big established banks. They can struggle to get access to the payment systems and information they need, or face rules designed for a big bank even when they are offering a much simpler service.

New businesses can take on the big four one service at a time - payments, digital wallets, and more. But right now, the rules are stacked against them. The laws that keep banks safe can also keep competitors out, and the big banks control the systems new players need to access. Labour will change that.

We'll make it easier for good Kiwi ideas to develop, while keeping strong protections for customers and the financial system.

### What Labour will change

#### More businesses will be able to compete with the big banks

Major banks will have to give smaller competitors fair access to the payment systems and banking information they need to offer new services.

#### Kiwi fintechs will have a simpler way to get started

A business offering things like digital wallets, prepaid cards or payment services won't have to become a full bank before it can compete.

Labour will create rules that match what the business actually does, with strong protections for customers. That gives innovative New Zealand businesses a better chance to get off the ground, attract investment, grow and create jobs.

#### Successful new businesses will have room to grow

We'll create a clear pathway for a payments company to develop into a digital bank, so New Zealand fintech can grow. National has held fintechs back. Labour will license them to compete with a new digital banking licence.

#### Payments will be faster

Labour will deliver secure, 24/7 real-time payments for fintechs by 2030, so money can move when businesses need it to.

#### Switching and signing up will be easier

If you choose to, you'll be able to use government-verified identity when joining a provider, cutting paperwork and making it easier to move to a better deal.

#### It will be easier to compare insurance

We'll open up insurance information too, starting with clearer, more standard terms for car and life insurance, helping people compare what they're actually getting.

### Kiwibank stays Kiwi

Labour created Kiwibank to bring more competition into banking.

It has an important role to play in challenging the big four and offering New Zealanders more choice.

Under Labour, Kiwibank will remain 100% New Zealand-owned.

### A better deal for New Zealand

These are practical changes to give Kiwis more choice, make banking easier and make banks work harder for their customers.

More competition means downward pressure on prices and better services. It means more options for small businesses. And it means Kiwi entrepreneurs with good ideas have a better chance to get started, grow and create jobs here.

National promised to shake up banking. Three years later, the biggest banks are still calling the shots.

Labour will open up banking, bring in more competition and give Kiwis a better chance of getting a better deal. It's part of our wider plan to lower everyday costs - alongside cracking down on price gouging and hidden fees, taking on the supermarket giants and cutting household bills.

Frequently asked questions
How much of the banking market do the big four banks control?
ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac together hold around 85 to 90 percent of registered bank assets in New Zealand, and their profits are high compared with banks overseas.

How does this affect small businesses?
Small businesses can often pay around 4.5 percentage points more in interest than big businesses. The big banks are also putting a smaller share of their lending into businesses while focusing more heavily on mortgages, making it harder for a good Kiwi business to get the backing it needs to grow.

How will Labour help New Zealand fintech businesses compete?
Major banks will have to give smaller competitors fair access to the payment systems and banking information they need. A business offering digital wallets, prepaid cards or payment services won't have to become a full bank first - Labour will create rules that match what the business actually does, with strong protections for customers.

What is the new digital banking licence?
Labour will create a clear pathway, through a new digital banking licence, for a payments company to develop into a digital bank as it grows, so successful New Zealand fintechs have room to expand and compete with the big four.

When will real-time payments be available?
Labour will deliver secure, 24/7 real-time payments for fintechs by 2030, so money can move when businesses need it to.

Will Kiwibank be sold or change ownership?
No. Under Labour, Kiwibank will remain 100% New Zealand-owned. Labour created Kiwibank to bring more competition into banking, and it will continue to play a role challenging the big four and offering New Zealanders more choice.

What changes for switching banks or comparing insurance?
Customers will be able to use government-verified identity when joining a new provider if they choose to, cutting paperwork and making it easier to switch. Labour will also open up insurance information, starting with clearer, more standard terms for car and life insurance, to help people compare what they're actually getting.

Good for customers. Good for Kiwi businesses. Good for jobs.

Better starts now.

documents/banning-price-gouging.md.title: Banning Price Gouging
documents/banning-price-gouging.md.text:
## Banning Price Gouging

Labour will make price gouging illegal, so big companies can't use their market power to overcharge you for the essentials.

Key facts
- Price gouging becomes illegal. There is currently no law against excessive price gouging in New Zealand
- Clear legal tests. For the first time, the law will define when high prices become unfair and excessive
- Covers the essentials: food and groceries, energy, fuel, telecommunications, banking, and insurance
- Only applies to big companies with significant market power, not your local dairy, cafe or tradie
- The Commerce Commission gets new powers to investigate dominant companies and take them to court
- Money paid back. Companies that overcharge will face penalties and be ordered to repay what they took
- Suppliers protected too. Labour will act when powerful companies unfairly squeeze growers, producers and suppliers

New Zealanders are working hard. They deserve a fair price for the essentials.

But when only a handful of big companies control the things people need, like groceries, power and fuel, they have the power to charge unfair prices, simply because customers have nowhere else to go.

Right now, there's no law against excessive price gouging. Labour will change that, so that the big companies can't rip you off, and you and your family can save more money.

### What we'll do

Labour will crack down on big companies who charge excessive prices for essential goods and services.

We'll also act when powerful companies unfairly squeeze the growers, producers, and other suppliers people rely on.

### Why it matters

Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living, but he has made it worse. One in three New Zealand households couldn't afford enough food last year.

People are working harder but still going backwards. When companies have too much power, the government should stop them using it to rip people off.

Only Labour will act.

### How it works

#### Make price gouging illegal

Labour will change the law so companies can't exploit their market power to overcharge people for the essentials.

#### Set clear legal tests

For the first time, the law will define when high prices become unfair and excessive. When prices are well above what it costs a company to supply, or well above what the same goods cost in a competitive market, large companies could face penalties and repay the consumers they have overcharged.

#### Give the Commerce Commission the power to act

The Commerce Commission will have the power to investigate what dominant companies are charging and take them to court.

#### Let consumer and supplier groups bring forward cases

Groups acting for consumers, growers, or suppliers will be able to take complaints to the Commerce Commission.

#### Take the profit out of price gouging

Big companies that use their market power to charge unfair and excessive prices will face penalties and be ordered to give what they overcharged back to people. A company thinking about ripping New Zealanders off will know that if they're caught, they'll have to pay back every dollar.

### Who will it cover?

#### Only the big players

The law will apply where a company has enough market power that customers can't realistically switch, suppliers have nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggle to enter the market. The policy doesn't touch your local dairy, cafe or tradie. Investment, innovation, and improvements that help with supply will also be protected.

#### Only essential goods and services

The law will stop New Zealanders being ripped off paying for:

- Food and groceries
- Energy
- Fuel
- Telecommunications
- Banking
- Insurance

Frequently asked questions
What is price gouging and is it currently illegal in New Zealand?
Price gouging is when a company uses its market power to charge excessive prices for goods or services that customers cannot do without. Right now there is no law against excessive price gouging in New Zealand. Labour will change that.

How will the law define an unfair or excessive price?
For the first time, the law will define when high prices become unfair and excessive. Where prices are well above what it costs a company to supply, or well above what the same goods cost in a competitive market, large companies could face penalties and be required to repay the consumers they have overcharged.

Which goods and services will be covered?
The law will cover essential goods and services: food and groceries, energy, fuel, telecommunications, banking, and insurance.

Which companies will the law apply to?
Only the big players. The law will apply where a company has enough market power that customers cannot realistically switch, suppliers have nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggle to enter the market.

Will this affect small businesses?
No. The policy does not touch your local dairy, cafe or tradie. It only applies to companies with significant market power in essential goods and services.

What powers will the Commerce Commission have?
The Commerce Commission will have the power to investigate what dominant companies are charging and take them to court. Groups acting for consumers, growers or suppliers will also be able to take complaints to the Commerce Commission.

What happens to companies that break the law?
Big companies that use their market power to charge unfair and excessive prices will face penalties and be ordered to give back what they overcharged. A company considering overcharging New Zealanders will know that if it is caught, it will have to pay back every dollar.

Does this protect suppliers and growers as well as consumers?
Yes. Labour will also act when powerful companies unfairly squeeze the growers, producers and other suppliers people rely on, and supplier groups will be able to bring complaints to the Commerce Commission.

Will this discourage investment or innovation?
No. Investment, innovation, and improvements that help with supply will be protected under the law.

A fair price for the things you can't do without - and just the start of how life will get better with Labour.

Better starts now.

## A Better Deal When You Fly

Labour will make sure the price you see is the price you pay, you get your money back when things go wrong, and more airlines compete for your business.

Key facts
- Full price upfront. Airlines must show every fee included, and tell you when your personal data is used to set your price
- Automatic refunds when a big airline cancels or significantly changes your flight, plus compensation for badly delayed bags
- Major airlines must publish reliability data on delays, cancellations and baggage handling
- Major airlines must give the Commerce Commission information on fares, costs and profits, reported regularly
- Fair access to airport infrastructure for every airline, and an end to airports overcharging for parking and food
- Aimed at big airlines, not small regional carriers like Sounds Air or Air Chathams

For many New Zealanders, flying isn't a luxury. It's how you get to work, see family, get to a medical appointment or run your business.

But flying is expensive. On some routes, fares have gone up by nearly 300%. And on many regional routes, there's only one airline to choose from.

New Zealanders should get a better deal when they fly.

Labour is on the side of hardworking New Zealanders who want a fair deal, whether you rely on airlines to get around, or are a smaller Kiwi airline trying to get a foothold.

### What Labour will change

#### You'll see the real price before you book

Airlines will have to show the full price, with every fee included, so you can easily compare airlines. They'll also have to tell you when they use your personal data, like your search history, to set the price you're offered.

#### You'll get your money back if something goes wrong

If a big airline cancels your flight or changes it significantly, you'll get an automatic refund. If your checked bag is badly delayed, or you pay for something you don't get, you'll be compensated or reimbursed. These rules are aimed at big airlines, not small regional carriers like Sounds Air or Air Chathams.

#### You'll know which airlines you can rely on

Major airlines will have to publish how often their flights are delayed or cancelled, and how reliable they are at handling your bags.

#### You'll be able to see if fares are fair

Major airlines will have to give the Commerce Commission information on their fares, costs and profits, and it will be reported regularly. That means you can see what's really driving the price of your ticket.

#### You'll have more airlines to choose from

Smaller airlines can struggle to get fair access to airport gates, check-in, baggage handling and ground services. Labour will make sure every airline gets fair access to airport infrastructure.

We'll also update the rules that let airlines link up their flights, so smaller airlines can reach more passengers, including people connecting from international flights.

#### You'll pay fairer prices at the airport

The cost of your trip isn't just the price of your ticket. We'll stop airports using their local monopoly to overcharge you for parking, food and other services.

#### Airport upgrades shouldn't push up your fare

Airports need to invest in terminals and runways, and those costs can end up in your ticket price. Labour will look at ways to help regulated airports borrow more cheaply, so there's less pressure on what you pay.

### Why it matters

New Zealand's size and geography mean flying will always be important. For many journeys there simply isn't a practical alternative.

There are good reasons why flying in New Zealand can cost more, including fuel, maintenance and the cost of operating smaller aircraft on shorter routes. But that doesn't fully explain the big price rises we've seen in recent years.

The Commerce Commission has found that on many regional routes, Air New Zealand faces limited or no competition. When one airline has a route to itself, there's little pressure to keep fares down or improve service.

When the big players dominate the market, you end up paying more than you should. Labour will change that. We will give smaller Kiwi airlines a fair go, so the big airlines have to work harder for your business.

With more airlines competing for your business, you'll get more choice, better prices and better services.

### Keeping your region connected

Reliable air services matter enormously to regional New Zealand. They help people get to appointments, see family and travel for work. They also help businesses reach customers, move goods and connect with the rest of the country.

But some smaller routes can struggle to remain viable, putting communities at risk of losing important connections. Some smaller routes will always be hard to run at a profit. We shouldn't wait until a route is about to disappear before acting.

Labour will bring together airlines, airports and local leaders to find lasting ways to keep essential routes running, learning from what already works in places like Australia and Europe.

### A real fix, not a short-term one

National's answer is short-term support for smaller airlines and a voluntary charter for passengers, while leaving the underlying problems in place. Labour will fix the rules to make sure you get a better deal, and smaller airlines have a fair shot.

This is part of how Labour will bring costs down right across the economy. Whether it's supermarkets, banks, airlines, or getting your car fixed, we'll make sure smaller businesses can compete and get you a better deal.

And to make getting around cheaper, we'll also freeze fuel tax for three years, and cap public transport fares at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 a week everywhere else.

Whether you drive, catch the bus or train, or fly, Labour will make sure you can get where you're going for less.

Frequently asked questions
Why are airfares so high in New Zealand?
There are good reasons flying in New Zealand can cost more, including fuel, maintenance and the cost of operating smaller aircraft on shorter routes. But that doesn't fully explain the big price rises of recent years, with fares on some routes up nearly 300%. The Commerce Commission has found that on many regional routes, Air New Zealand faces limited or no competition, which means little pressure to keep fares down or improve service.

What will airlines have to show me before I book?
Airlines will have to show the full price with every fee included, so you can easily compare airlines. They will also have to tell you when they use your personal data, such as your search history, to set the price you're offered.

When will I get a refund?
If a big airline cancels your flight or changes it significantly, you'll get an automatic refund. If your checked bag is badly delayed, or you pay for something you don't get, you'll be compensated or reimbursed.

Which airlines do the refund and reporting rules apply to?
The refund and reporting rules are aimed at big airlines, not small regional carriers like Sounds Air or Air Chathams. Labour's competition measures are designed to give smaller airlines a fair go.

How will I know which airlines are reliable and whether fares are fair?
Major airlines will have to publish how often their flights are delayed or cancelled, and how reliable they are at handling bags. They will also have to give the Commerce Commission information on their fares, costs and profits, which will be reported regularly, so you can see what's really driving the price of your ticket.

How will Labour increase competition between airlines?
Labour will make sure every airline gets fair access to airport infrastructure, including gates, check-in, baggage handling and ground services. Labour will also update the rules that let airlines link up their flights, so smaller airlines can reach more passengers, including people connecting from international flights.

How will Labour stop airports overcharging?
Labour will stop airports using their local monopoly to overcharge for parking, food and other services. Labour will also look at ways to help regulated airports borrow more cheaply to invest in terminals and runways, so there is less pressure on ticket prices.

How will Labour keep regional routes connected?
Labour will bring together airlines, airports and local leaders to find lasting ways to keep essential regional routes running, learning from what already works in places like Australia and Europe, rather than waiting until a route is about to disappear.

How is this different from National's approach?
National's answer is short-term support for smaller airlines and a voluntary charter for passengers, while leaving the underlying problems in place. Labour will fix the rules so passengers get a better deal and smaller airlines have a fair shot.

Whether you drive, catch the bus or train, or fly, Labour will make sure you can get where you're going for less.

documents/capitalgainstax.md.title: Capital Gains Tax to Level the Playing Field for Businesses, Create Jobs and Fix New Zealand's Health System
documents/capitalgainstax.md.text:
## Capital Gains Tax

A simple, targeted capital gains tax on commercial or residential property (excluding the family home or farm). Every dollar raised will be used to fix New Zealand's health system, including three free doctor's visits each year for every New Zealander.

Key facts
- What's covered: commercial property and residential investment property only
- What's exempt: the family home (including lifestyle blocks), farms, inheritances, KiwiSaver, shares, businesses, and personal items
- When it starts: no tax on gains before 1 July 2027; applies only to profits made after that date, and only when the property is sold
- Rate: 28%, aligned with the company tax rate, so property profits are taxed like other business income
- Who pays: nine in 10 New Zealanders won't pay any tax on the property they own
- Where the money goes: 100% to health, including three free doctor's visits each year for every New Zealander

### Here's how Labour's plan works

#### What's included

A 28 percent tax on any profit made after 1 July 2027 when a commercial or residential property (excluding the family home) is sold. Not a single dollar of profit made before 1 July 2027 will be taxed.

##### Quick example

A commercial building is purchased on 1 July 2025 for $400,000. On 1 July 2027 it is valued at $600,000, and it is later sold for $700,000. The tax applies only to the $100,000 gain after 1 July 2027.

#### What is exempt

Everything else. Your family home (including lifestyle blocks) and farms will be tax-free. KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, gifts, and personal items like cars, boats, art, and furniture are all exempt. Small businesses selling their premises to buy a bigger one will not be taxed.

#### Who pays

Nine out of 10 New Zealanders do not own more than one property or a commercial property, so they won't pay the tax.

#### Where the money goes

Every dollar raised will be ring-fenced to provide all New Zealanders with better healthcare, starting with three free doctor's visits each year for all New Zealanders.

#### Why it works

It rewards work and productive investment and puts businesses that create jobs and drive innovation on a level playing field, rather than speculation on multiple properties.

#### What other countries do

New Zealand is one of the only countries in the world without some form of capital gains tax. Australia introduced a capital gains tax in 1985, and its economy and incomes have kept growing.

“You only need to look across the Tasman or to any other countries that have capital gains tax and see that they are not less productive, they are more productive than us.”

— Tax expert, Professor Craig Elliffe

### Why is a capital gains tax being proposed?

New Zealand cannot build a strong economy through buying and selling property alone. We build it by rewarding work, backing Kiwi businesses - and making sure everyone can see a doctor when they need to.

Right now, too much of our wealth is locked in property, not in the productive economy that lifts wages and creates jobs. And one in six New Zealanders can't afford to see a doctor.

A simple, targeted capital gains tax will unlock investment so more capital goes into businesses, innovation, and jobs. Every dollar raised will be ring-fenced for our health system and fund three free doctor's visits for everyone each year.

### Examples

##### Example 1: Jim and Pat

Jim and Pat have owned one property, their family home, for 25 years. They initially purchased it for $300,000. As it is their family home, they don't need to value it on 1 July 2027. In 2030, they decide to downsize and sell their home. At the time of sale, it is valued at $1.5 million.

Tax outcome: as this is their only property, Jim and Pat will not pay any tax.

##### Example 2: Sarah and Michael

Sarah and Michael own multiple investment properties. In 2018, they purchased their fourth property for $750,000. On 1 July 2027, the property is valued at $900,000. Sarah and Michael sell the property in 2029 for $1.2 million.

Tax outcome: only the increase after 1 July 2027 will be taxed at 28%.

Frequently asked questions
What if I've made a loss on my property since I bought it?
- A property can be valued at either its purchase price, or the value at the date the CGT is introduced, whichever is higher.
- This will ensure the tax is only applied to the gain in value from 1 July 2027, not paper gains.

What if I have made capital improvements to a property?
- The cost of additions and improvements can be included in the property’s total cost, so you won’t pay capital gains tax on money you’ve spent improving it, as long as you haven’t claimed depreciation on that work.

What value should I use at the start date of the capital gains tax?
- The default value for any property when the capital gains tax starts will be its rateable value. If you think that is too low, you can get a registered valuation instead.
- This can be done later, as long it is the value of the property on 1 July 2027 and completed before you sell.

Won't this increase rents?
- Landlords charge what the market allows. Rents are set by supply and demand, not by a tax paid years later when a property is sold.
- Decades of international evidence shows there is little impact on rent from a CGT. Rents do not go up because someone pays tax on a future sale.

What will this do to house prices?
- New Zealand won't get wealthier if we are only buying and selling houses from each other.
- We need to direct more investment into the productive parts of the economy. Fewer investors bidding against first home buyers is a good thing.

Is my KiwiSaver affected?
- No. KiwiSaver and businesses are exempt from the capital gains tax.
- Saying businesses that KiwiSaver invests in will be subject to the tax is false.
- Businesses that buy and sell property already pay tax - this changes nothing for them.

Will this tax small businesses?
- The tax only applies to residential and commercial property; it does not apply to the businesses themselves.
- Most small businesses lease their buildings, so are not subject to the tax.
- Some do own their property, and if they make improvements, that will be deductible.
- If they want to sell and move into a bigger property, there is no tax to pay.

What if a small business decides to sell its premises and move to a bigger one?
- They will not pay any tax.
- Our plan is about growing the economy and investing to help turn great ideas into profitable businesses that create jobs.

Doesn't New Zealand already tax more than Australia, and won't this make it worse?
- Australia introduced a capital gains tax in 1985, and its economy and incomes have kept growing.
- The issue isn't a capital gains tax or not - it's how we design the system to make it work for everyone.
- Labour's plan will shift investment from property speculation into the productive economy.

Three free doctor's visits for everyone, paid for with a simple, targeted capital gains tax.

documents/cervicalscreening.md.text:
## Free Cervical Screening

From 1 October 2027, cervical screening will be free for everyone aged 25-69 through Labour's Medicard, alongside three free doctor's visits every year for every New Zealander.

Key facts
- Free cervical screening for everyone aged 25-69
- Starts 1 October 2027
- Eligibility automatically loaded onto the Medicard
- Available at your local doctor or community screening events - just scan your Medicard
- Free screening is in addition to three free doctor's visits a year
- Cost: $21.6 million for the first full year, funded from existing health baselines

### Why this matters

Cervical cancer is among the most preventable cancers yet 85 percent of those diagnosed have never been screened or missed screenings.

Free cervical screening means more on-time screening, earlier diagnosis, lives saved, and less pressure on our hospitals. It also brings cervical screening in line with other nationwide free cancer screening programmes.

### The cost of waiting

Cost should never be a barrier to care. Under Christopher Luxon, it's become harder and more expensive to see a doctor. He promised to fix the cost of living, but it's getting worse and there's no plan to fix our health system. It doesn't have to be this way.

### How much it will cost

Cervical screening for everyone who needs it aged 25-69 will be available from 1 October 2027 and will cost $21.6 million for the first full year. It will be funded from existing health baselines.

Labour will build a health system that keeps people healthy, not just treats them when they're sick.

Frequently asked questions
Who is eligible for free cervical screening?
Everyone aged 25 to 69.

When does it start?
From 1 October 2027.

How do I access it?
Eligibility is automatically loaded onto your Medicard - simply scan it at your local doctor or a community screening event.

How much will this cost, and how is it funded?
$21.6 million for the first full year, funded from existing health baselines.

Is this on top of my free doctor's visits?
Yes - free cervical screening is in addition to the three free doctor's visits every New Zealander gets each year.

Money back in your pocket and just one of the ways Labour policies will make your life better.

documents/community-housing-and-retireme.text:
## Community Housing and Retirement Villages

Labour will require retirement villages to repay residents within three months, and back community housing with a $950 million Crown guarantee.

Key facts
- Retirement villages must repay residents within three months, and this applies to all residents, not just new ones
- Independent disputes resolution service for retirement village residents
- Protection for genuinely vulnerable small, rural and charitable villages, without a loophole for larger operators
- $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency (CHFA), from Labour's first Budget in Government in 2027
- Cheaper finance, more homes: CHFA estimates that for every 11 homes built, the financing efficiency could pay for a twelfth, at no additional cost to the taxpayer

### Retirement villages

Seniors deserve certainty and fair treatment when they leave a retirement village.

Labour will require retirement villages to repay residents within three months, so seniors and their families aren't left waiting indefinitely for money that belongs to them. This will apply to all residents, not just new ones.

We'll establish a simple, accessible and independent disputes resolution service so residents have somewhere to turn when things go wrong.

We'll protect genuinely vulnerable small, rural and charitable villages without creating a loophole that lets larger operators avoid their responsibilities.

### Crown guarantee for community housing

After three years of neglect, New Zealand's housing shortage is getting worse. One of the fastest and most effective ways to build more homes is to reduce the cost of finance for the organisations already doing the work.

Labour will provide a $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency (CHFA). It is similar to the guarantee provided to banks and would only be called on in the unlikely event of a default. The community housing sector was hoping the current Government would provide this guarantee. They didn't, but Labour will.

By enabling AAA-rated borrowing, interest rates for housing providers are cut, and those savings are invested in building more homes. The maths is straightforward: CHFA estimates that for every 11 homes built, the financing efficiency could pay for a twelfth, at no additional cost to the taxpayer.

Frequently asked questions
What will Labour do for retirement village residents?
Labour will require retirement villages to repay residents within three months, so seniors and their families aren't left waiting indefinitely for money that belongs to them. Labour will also establish a simple, accessible and independent disputes resolution service.

Will the three-month repayment rule apply to existing residents?
Yes. The three-month repayment requirement will apply to all residents, not just new ones.

What is the disputes resolution service for retirement villages?
Labour will establish a simple, accessible and independent disputes resolution service so residents have somewhere to turn when things go wrong.

Will small, rural and charitable retirement villages be treated differently?
Labour will protect genuinely vulnerable small, rural and charitable villages without creating a loophole that lets larger operators avoid their responsibilities.

What is Labour's Crown guarantee for community housing?
Labour will provide a $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency (CHFA), effective from Labour's first Budget in 2027.

How will the Crown guarantee help build more homes?
By enabling AAA-rated borrowing, interest rates for housing providers are cut, and those savings are invested in building more homes.

Why is Labour providing the guarantee?
After three years of neglect, New Zealand's housing shortage is getting worse. One of the fastest and most effective ways to build more homes is to reduce the cost of finance for the organisations already doing the work.

Every New Zealander deserves a safe, secure, affordable place to call home.

documents/cost-of-living-plan.md.text:
## Labour's Cost of Living Plan

Our promise What you could save Healthcare Getting around Power bills Kids to school Fairer prices Getting ahead Fully costed FAQs
Getting the cost of living under control will be Labour's number one priority. That means action on the bills you face now and making sure you get a better deal in the future.

Our promise to New Zealanders
- Give every New Zealander three free GP visits a year with a new Medicard and Medicard App
- Guarantee every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse a job
- Freeze fuel tax for three years
- Cap public transport fares at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 everywhere else
- Make price gouging by the big companies illegal, including on groceries, fuel and power, and force companies to pay you back if they are found to have overcharged you
- Cut student debt by 10% on 1 April 2027, or for students who choose to stay and work in New Zealand for three years after they finish their study
- Scrap the $5 prescription charge
- Support households to install solar with low-interest SolarSaver loans
- Crack down on hidden fees and subscription traps
- Get Kiwis back into work by fixing schools and hospitals, backing 30,000 apprentices and creating jobs for local tradies

Getting the cost of living under control isn't just about bringing prices down. It's also about making sure people have enough money coming in to cover their bills.

Labour will also get Kiwis back into work and change the rules so smaller Kiwi businesses have a fair chance to compete with the big companies. Our plan means lower bills, more good jobs and reliable incomes, and a fairer deal for New Zealanders.

Every dollar is costed. Every dollar is funded. You deserve to see where the money comes from, so we've produced an independently reviewed financial plan. See Labour's Fiscal Plan →

### What better means for your household

Labour's plan will put money back in your pocket. Not everyone will benefit from every policy. But a family benefiting from just some could be thousands of dollars better off every year.

| Commitment | What you could save |
| --- | --- |
| Three free GP visits | $183 per person a year, $366 for a couple |
| Free prescriptions | $5 per item |
| Fare caps | Around $25 a week, or around $1,300 a year ($2,600 for a couple) |
| Freezing fuel tax | $520 a year by 2030 for the average family |
| Free maternity scans | $180 for a straightforward pregnancy |
| SolarSaver | Around $1,000 a year |
| Student debt cut | 10% cut from whatever you owe |

### Why it matters

+21%Cost of the average GP visit in three years

+25%Power bills in three years

1 in 6New Zealanders can't afford to see a doctor when they're sick

155,000New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they needed last year

### 1. Better means healthcare you can afford

You shouldn't have to put off seeing a doctor or leave your prescription at the pharmacy because you can't afford it. The cost of seeing a GP has gone up 21% in three years. One in six New Zealanders can't afford to see a doctor when they're sick. And National has only increased the number of nurses by 54 in the last two years.

Labour will:

- Give every New Zealander three free GP visits a year with a new Medicard or Medicard App
- Remove the $5 prescription charge from 1 July 2027
- Make cervical screening free for everyone aged 25 to 69 from 1 October 2027
- Make maternity scans free everywhere from July 2028

### 2. Better means getting around for less

Whether you're filling up the car, catching the bus or train, or flying to visit friends, the cost of getting around adds up. We'll help bring that cost down.

Labour will:

- Cap weekly public transport fares at $20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch and $10 everywhere else from 1 July 2027, saving the average commuter $25 a week, or $1,300 a year ($2,600 for a couple)
- Freeze fuel excise tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030
- Make it illegal for fuel companies to overcharge you for petrol and diesel - and force companies to pay you back if they are found to have overcharged you
- Make airlines show the full price upfront, so the price you see is the price you pay
- Guarantee refunds when a major airline cancels or significantly changes your flight
- Help smaller airlines compete

### 3. Better means lower power bills

Power bills have gone up 25% in three years. Labour will take action to stop companies overcharging you and make it easier to install solar without the upfront cost.

Labour will:

- Offer government-backed, low-interest SolarSaver loans for solar panels and batteries, saving the average household around $1,000 a year on power bills
- Give low- and middle-income households up to $3,000 in extra support
- Make sure people who rent can benefit through plug-in solar
- Make overcharging you for electricity illegal, and make companies found doing so pay you back

### 4. Better means cutting the cost of getting kids to school

School costs add up - lunches and long drives to get the kids to the classroom. We'll help parents with those bills.

Labour will:

- Cap public transport fares so kids can get to school for less
- Bring back fresh, locally made school lunches from Term 1 2028
- Work to restore the rural school bus routes that National cut

### 5. Better means fairer prices

When a few big companies dominate a market, they can charge too much because customers have nowhere else to go. Labour will take on unfair prices and fees - and give smaller businesses the chance to challenge them.

Labour will:

- Make the big supermarkets open up wholesale supply so smaller stores can compete and you get a better deal at the checkout
- Change the law to make price gouging on essentials like power and petrol illegal, and to make companies pay you back what they overcharged
- Ban hidden fees so there are no surprise charges when you book flights or buy tickets online - the price you see will be the price you pay
- Make cancelling subscriptions and switching providers easy, so you can cancel your gym or streaming subscription as easily as you signed up
- Ban junk insurance and secret finance commissions at car yards
- Introduce a Right to Repair law so you have more choice over who fixes your car, helping keep repair costs down
- Give independent mechanics, service stations, digital banks, and regional airlines a fair shot

### 6. Better means help to get ahead

It's hard to get ahead when you're weighed down by student debt, out of work, or unsure whether your pay will cover the bills. We'll back people to learn, earn and build a future here.

Labour will:

- Guarantee New Zealand-trained graduate nurses a job
- Cut student debt by 10% on 1 April 2027 or for students who choose to stay and work in New Zealand for three years after they finish their study
- Clear student loans of $2,000 or less completely
- Expand Apprenticeship Boost to get 30,000 more people learning on the job
- Give apprentices and tradies a $1,000 tools grant
- Fix schools and hospitals, creating work for local tradies and builders

### Fully costed and paid for

Government is about choices. You should be able to see what we're promising and how we'll pay for it. Labour has published an independently reviewed Fiscal Plan setting out, line by line, how every election commitment will be funded.

As Finance Minister in a Labour Government, Barbara Edmonds, an expert tax lawyer, will:

- Pay for our commitments within the same pot of money National has set aside for future budgets
- Fund announced capital commitments within the $12 billion National has set aside for future capital allowances, leaving almost $8 billion of that capital funding unallocated
- Return the Government's books to surplus in 2028/29
- Bring net debt down towards 20% of GDP over time

#### Our health commitments

Three free GP visits, free prescriptions, free maternity scans and free cervical screening are funded through Labour's targeted capital gains tax. It applies to gains on investment and commercial property, while excluding the family home, farms, businesses and KiwiSaver. Nine out of ten New Zealanders will not pay it. Every dollar raised from the tax is invested in health.

#### Our other commitments

- The public transport fare cap is funded by reprioritising 1% of the National Land Transport Fund, while continuing investment in roads and public transport.
- SolarSaver is funded by reprioritising existing government funding.
- The student debt reduction is included in Labour's capital commitments.

Getting the cost of living under control and managing the books carefully aren't competing goals. We'll do both.

### Better means getting your costs under control

Kiwis are working hard. You should be able to put food on the table, afford to see a doctor and get where you need to go - with something left over at the end of the week.

We'll bring bills down, get people back into work and help young New Zealanders build a future here. Good jobs and decent pay are how families get ahead.

We'll also give Kiwi businesses - from local mechanics to independent grocers and new banking providers - a proper chance to take on the big players. When local firms can grow and employ more people, and customers have more choice, the whole country gets a better deal.

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's Cost of Living Plan?
Labour's Cost of Living Plan is a package of policies to help with the bills New Zealanders face every week - food, power, transport, healthcare and the cost of getting kids to school - and to crack down on big companies overcharging customers.

Getting the cost of living under control will be Labour's number one priority, with action on the bills people face now, more good jobs and reliable incomes, and a fairer deal for New Zealanders.

Every commitment is costed and funded in Labour's Fiscal Plan.

How much could my household save under Labour's plan?
Not everyone will benefit from every policy, but Labour says a family benefiting from just some of them could be thousands of dollars better off every year. Labour's estimates are:

- Three free GP visits: $183 per person each year ($366 for a couple)
- Free prescriptions: $5 per item
- Public transport fare cap: around $25 a week, or around $1,300 a year ($2,600 for a couple)
- Freezing fuel tax: $520 a year by 2030 for the average family
- Free maternity scans: $180 for a straightforward pregnancy
- SolarSaver: around $1,000 a year on power bills
- Student debt cut: 10% off whatever you owe

What free healthcare will I get, and when does it start?
The average GP visit costs 21% more than it did three years ago, and one in six New Zealanders can't afford to see a doctor when they're sick.

A Labour Government will take action to make healthcare affordable:

- Every New Zealander will get three free GP visits a year at their enrolled practice through a new Medicard and Medicard App from July 2028.
- The $5 prescription charge will be removed from 1 July 2027.
- Cervical screening will be free for everyone aged 25 to 69 from 1 October 2027.
- Referred maternity scans will be free everywhere in New Zealand from July 2028.

How much will the public transport fare cap save me?
From 1 July 2027, the most you'll pay each week will be $20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 everywhere else. Once you reach the weekly cap, your remaining eligible trips that week are free.

Labour estimates a regular passenger could save around $25 a week and up to $1,300 a year, or $2,600 for a couple. The cap also applies to kids using public transport to get to school.

What is Labour's fuel tax freeze?
Labour will freeze fuel excise tax for three years, which Labour estimates saves an average family $520 a year by 2030. World oil prices will still go up and down, but a Labour Government won't add more fuel tax at the pump.

Labour will also show whether fuel companies pass on lower oil prices when their costs fall, and fuel companies found overcharging will have to pay customers back.

How will Labour bring down my power bill?
Labour will offer government-backed, low-interest SolarSaver loans for solar panels and batteries with no upfront cost, saving a typical household around $1,000 a year.

Low- and middle-income households can get a kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000, and renters can access the subsidy for plug-in solar - a two-panel kit costs around $1,500, saves $300-$400 a year on power bills, and pays for itself in four to five years.

Labour will also make overcharging for electricity illegal and make companies found doing so pay customers back.

How is Labour helping with the cost of getting kids to school?
From Term 1 2028, Labour will bring back fresh, locally made school lunches for children in the school lunch programme, continuing to cover 244,400 students in the 1,014 schools already included. Lunches will be funded at $5 a meal, and $6.50 for students in Years 9 to 13, and made in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners, or by local caterers.

Labour will also work to restore all of the rural school bus routes that have been cut, or find a suitable alternative with rural communities and local councils if a route can't be restored. The public transport fare cap will also help kids get to school for less.

How will Labour stop big companies overcharging?
Labour will make price gouging illegal for essentials including food, power, fuel, banking and insurance, with the Commerce Commission able to investigate and make companies pay back what they overcharged.

Labour will also make big supermarkets supply smaller competitors on fair terms and ban junk fees charged to suppliers, ban hidden fees and make cancelling subscriptions as easy as signing up, ban junk insurance and secret finance commissions at car yards, introduce a right to repair law starting with cars, and give independent mechanics, service stations, digital banks and regional airlines a fair shot.

These rules target powerful companies, not local businesses.

How is Labour helping people get ahead?
Labour will cut student debt by 10%:

- For graduates who have finished study and are repaying their loans, the cut applies on 1 April 2027
- For current and future students, the cut applies after spending three years in New Zealand following their study

Eligible balances of $2,000 or less cleared completely after meeting the three-year requirement.

Labour will also expand Apprenticeship Boost to get 30,000 apprentices into work with a $1,000 toolbox grant, guarantee eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurses a job, and fix schools and hospitals, creating work for local builders, tradies and apprentices.

How is Labour's Cost of Living Plan paid for?
Every dollar is costed and funded in Labour's independently reviewed Fiscal Plan:

- Three free GP visits, free prescriptions, free maternity scans and free cervical screening are funded through Labour's targeted capital gains tax, which applies to gains on investment and commercial property (excluding the family home, farms, businesses and KiwiSaver)
- The public transport fare cap is funded by reprioritising 1% of the National Land Transport Fund
- SolarSaver is funded by reprioritising existing government funding, and the student debt reduction is included in Labour's capital commitments

Labour's commitments fit within the operating allowances already set aside for future Budgets and within the $12 billion of future capital allowances, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated, with a return to surplus in 2028/29 and net debt falling towards 20% of GDP over time.

When do these changes start?
- 1 April 2027: first student loan cut for graduates already repaying their loans (current and future students qualify after three years in New Zealand following their study)
- 1 July 2027: the $5 prescription charge removed and the weekly public transport fare cap begins
- 1 October 2027: free cervical screening for ages 25 to 69
- Term 1 2028: fresh, locally made school lunches return
- July 2028: three free GP visits
- July 2028: free referred maternity scans
- Fuel tax: fuel excise tax frozen for three years
- SolarSaver: loans, subsidies and EECA support up and running within 12 months of taking office

Better starts now.

On 7 November, Party Vote Labour.
