documents/fiscal-plan.md.text:
## Labour's Fiscal Plan

Better today. Better tomorrow. Every promise Labour has made is fully paid for.

Key facts
- Every election commitment is fully costed and fully funded, independently reviewed by Hall Chadwick
- Books return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2028/29
- Net debt down towards 20% of GDP over time
- Operating allowance held at $2.4 billion per Budget, as set at Budget 2026
- $12 billion in future capital allowances; Labour's commitments use $4.1 billion, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated
- $15.5 billion of additional health funding over the forecast period

Hard work should get you somewhere. If you work hard and do your bit, you should be able to get ahead and build a good life here in New Zealand. Right now, too many people are doing everything asked of them and still going backwards.

National promised to grow the economy and get the Government's finances in order. It has done neither - unemployment is higher, growth is weaker, debt has continued to rise, and frontline services have been cut.

Labour will balance the books without shrinking the economy. That means smarter investments, backing the people and businesses doing the work, and judging every dollar by whether it makes New Zealand stronger - not short-term cuts that put more people out of work or leave a bigger bill for the future.

### Four commitments

- Everything is paid for. Every election commitment fits within Budget 2027's $2.4 billion operating allowance and the $12 billion of future capital allowances.
- Make every dollar work harder. Investment is focused on what improves people's lives, strengthens the economy, or prevents bigger costs later.
- Balance the books while getting costs under control. A government can't call its fiscal policy a success if the books only look better because more people are out of work or services are run down.
- Grow the economy by backing the people doing the work. Labour will back productive investment, small businesses, skills, technology and infrastructure to grow the economy from the grassroots up.

### Capital commitments

Labour's announced capital commitments fit comfortably within the $12 billion of future capital allowances, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated.

| Commitment | Capital funding |
| --- | --- |
| New Zealand Future Fund | $200 million |
| Student loan write-off | $420 million |
| Hospitals | $200 million |
| Schools | $400 million |
| Kainga Ora housing (over four years) | $2.9 billion |
| Ratepayer Assistance Scheme solar expenditure | $7 million |

### Where the money goes

#### Health

Labour's plan puts $15.5 billion of additional funding into health over the forecast period, combining the health cost-pressure track from the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update with Labour's announced health commitments: three free GP visits a year through the Medicard, free prescriptions, free cervical screening, free maternity scans, and the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee. Every dollar raised from Labour's targeted Capital Gains Tax is invested in health.

#### Public services

Labour will reverse half of the additional cuts planned for the next Budget, and fully reverse the cuts National has planned for future Budgets. Agencies will still be expected to spend carefully and deliver value for money.

#### Pay equity

Labour will reinstate pay equity legislation and provide an immediate $4 an hour pay increase for care and support workers. This commitment is fully funded in this Fiscal Plan - see Labour's pay equity policy for full detail.

#### Small business

Labour will help small businesses invest, get invoices paid faster, cut unnecessary paperwork, and give Kiwi firms a fairer shot at government contracts, through the Small Business Action Plan and Small Business First.

#### Land Transport Fund

Labour will freeze fuel tax for three years and cap weekly public transport fares at $20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 everywhere else. Both commitments are fully funded in this Fiscal Plan, with the fare cap funded by reprioritising 1% of the National Land Transport Fund, so investment in roads and public transport continues.

### Key fiscal indicators

OBEGAL: Labour will return the Government's books to an operating surplus before gains and losses in 2028/29, using the standard OBEGAL measure rather than the OBEGALx measure introduced by the current Government.

Debt: Labour will bring net debt down below 20% of GDP over time. Net debt gives a fuller picture of the Crown's fiscal position because it recognises both financial assets and liabilities. Borrowing for high-value capital investment can be the sensible choice when the asset will serve New Zealanders for decades.

### Independent review

Hall Chadwick was commissioned by the New Zealand Labour Party to independently review this Fiscal Plan against the Budget allowances set out in the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (PREFU).

The review confirmed that the estimated spending, revenue, and capital expenditure are supported by the presented and announced policy material; the estimated spending, revenue, and capital expenditure are reasonable assessments, conditional on the underpinning assumptions of each policy and commitment; and the spending and revenue commitments fall within the stated fiscal strategy.

Frequently asked questions
Is every Labour election commitment funded?
Yes, every election commitment is fully costed and fully funded within its Fiscal Plan. The plan has been independently reviewed by accounting firm Hall Chadwick, which confirmed the estimated spending, revenue and capital expenditure are reasonable, conditional on the underlying assumptions, and fall within Labour's stated fiscal strategy.

When will Labour return the Budget to surplus?
Labour will return the Government's books to an OBEGAL (operating balance before gains and losses) surplus in 2028/29. Labour will use the standard OBEGAL measure rather than the OBEGALx measure introduced by the current Government.

What are Labour's operating and capital allowances?
Labour will keep the operating allowance at $2.4 billion per Budget, as set at Budget 2026. For capital, the allowances are $3.5 billion for Budget 2027, $3.5 billion for Budget 2028, and $5 billion for Budget 2029 - a total of $12 billion. Labour's announced capital commitments total around $4.1 billion, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated.

What are Labour's capital commitments?
Labour's announced capital commitments are: $200 million for the New Zealand Future Fund, $420 million for the student loan write-off, $200 million for hospitals, $400 million for schools, $2.9 billion for Kainga Ora housing (spread over four years), and $7 million for Ratepayer Assistance Scheme solar expenditure.

How much is Labour investing in health?
Labour's plan provides $15.5 billion of additional funding for health over the forecast period, combining the health cost-pressure track from the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update with Labour's announced health commitments. Every dollar raised from Labour's targeted capital gains tax is invested in health.

How will Labour bring down net debt?
Labour will bring net debt down below 20% of GDP over time, using the net debt measure, which accounts for both the Crown's financial assets and its liabilities.

Who reviewed Labour's Fiscal Plan?
Hall Chadwick was commissioned by the New Zealand Labour Party to independently review the Fiscal Plan. Hall Chadwick confirmed the estimated spending, revenue and capital expenditure are supported by Labour's announced policy material, are reasonable assessments conditional on each policy's underlying assumptions, and fall within Labour's stated fiscal strategy.

New Zealand doesn't have to choose between responsible finances and a better future.

We can have both. Better today. Better tomorrow.

documents/fiscal-strategy.md.text:
## Labour's Fiscal Strategy

Objectives Why now People at the centre Growing the economy Public services FAQs
Labour will balance the books, return to surplus by 2029/30, reduce net debt to 20% of GDP, and keep government spending and revenue sustainable.

Labour's fiscal objectives
- Return to surplus. An OBEGAL surplus by 2029/30, using the original OBEGAL measure rather than OBEGALx
- Bring down debt. Reduce net debt to around 20% of GDP over time
- Sustainable spending and revenue. Core Crown expenditure and revenue held at around 33% of GDP when the capital gains tax is fully implemented
- Transparency. A new Parliamentary Budget Office to independently analyse the books and every party's spending commitments
- Restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate: price stability and maximum sustainable employment
- Restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act

Labour is the party that believes hard work should get you somewhere. If you work hard, have a go and do your bit, you should be able to get ahead and build a good life here in New Zealand.

Right now, too many Kiwis don't have that chance. People are working hard and still going backwards.

New Zealand deserves better.

A Labour Government will focus on creating more and better jobs, making healthcare affordable and lowering household bills - because that's how more New Zealanders can get ahead, put down roots and build a future here at home.

That means balancing the books without shrinking the economy. It means spending smarter, investing where it pays off, and backing the people and businesses doing the work.

### Labour will:

#### Balance the books and return to surplus

Returning the original measure of OBEGAL, removing OBEGALx, Labour will return a surplus by 2029/30 and maintain a sustainable fiscal position over the forecast period. Labour's plan to return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2029/30 uses the same timing forecast in Budget 2026. Labour will return to a positive operating balance while still investing in the people, services and infrastructure New Zealand needs.

#### Bringing down debt

Labour will aim to reduce net debt down to 20% of GDP over time, and prioritise investments which support a strong growing economy. Net debt gives a better picture of the government's overall fiscal position because it recognises that the government also owns financial assets. This measure includes a wide range of government assets, such as the Super Fund and advances, and liabilities, including debt held by other Crown agencies like Kainga Ora.

#### Keep government spending and revenue sustainable

New Zealand should be making investments today so it can have a more productive tomorrow and reduce the debt burden in the future. That includes capital projects the country needs, like hospitals that don't leak, ferries that operate safely, and classrooms that aren't cold. Under Labour, core Crown expenditure and revenue will be maintained at around 33% of GDP when the capital gains tax is fully implemented.

#### Ensure fiscal transparency

We will establish a Parliamentary Budget Office to provide independent analysis of the government's books and election commitments, so all New Zealanders can see the trade-offs governments are making in their budgets.

### Time for a change

New Zealand cannot afford three more years of a National-led Government. They promised to fix things but after three years of fiscal mismanagement the country is worse off on almost every measure.

- Public services have been weakened by underinvestment and cuts to the frontline.
- Debt is higher, the return to surplus is further away than it was under Labour's forecasts, unemployment has climbed to near a decade-high, and too many families are finding it hard to make ends meet.
- Small businesses are under pressure, business confidence has been undermined, wages are failing to keep pace with rising costs, and more children are growing up without the basics.

Labour will balance the government's books without shrinking the economy.

A growing and resilient economy means governments can invest in quality healthcare, education, infrastructure, housing, and the public services that give people security and opportunity.

We will back New Zealand's potential by supporting businesses, especially the small businesses that are the heart of our economy, to grow and create good jobs, so people can build a future here, not overseas.

Labour has a proud record of managing the country's finances responsibly while investing in growth. We will continue that approach, investing in the things that make our economy stronger: more people in work, higher productivity, and public services that work for the people who pay for them.

### Putting people at the centre of fiscal and economic decision making

Economic policy should be judged by what it means for people's lives. Kiwis are working hard, doing the right things and playing by the rules, yet too many are still falling behind.

National has talked about economic growth while life has become harder and more expensive for the people that growth is supposed to benefit. Measures like GDP, inflation and debt are important, but they are not ends in themselves.

They matter because of what they mean for people: whether they have a good job, can afford the basics, access the services they need, and feel confident about their future.

#### Restoring wellbeing reporting

Labour will restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act, to ensure decisions take into account the impact on the lives and livelihoods of New Zealanders. Fiscal responsibility goes hand in hand with social responsibility. A government cannot claim success at managing the books if the result is higher unemployment, worsening services or poorer outcomes for New Zealanders.

Labour will use wellbeing measures alongside traditional economic measures to test whether government policies are actually helping New Zealanders get ahead: whether people have well-paid work, can cover the bills, are healthier and more secure, and feel confident about the future.

#### Restoring the Reserve Bank's dual mandate

Labour will restore the Reserve Bank dual mandate, so monetary policy is developed in a way that is consistent with two objectives: achieving and maintaining stability in the general level of prices over the medium term, and supporting maximum sustainable employment.

Keeping inflation in the target band is critical. High inflation squeezes household budgets and makes it harder for people and businesses to plan and invest. But unemployment has an outsized influence on those who lose their jobs, and on the wider economy and society.

Losing a job can be devastating for a family and damaging for the wider economy. It means less household spending, impacts on businesses, lost skills and experience, and lasting damage to productivity. It can also lead to higher demand for services like foodbanks, and more people sleeping rough. Prolonged unemployment can create lasting wage scarring, making it harder for people to get back on their feet and for the economy to reach its full potential.

Other countries, including the United States and Australia, continue to implement a dual mandate, keeping inflation low and stable while ensuring as many people as possible are in jobs. By restoring the Reserve Bank dual mandate and wellbeing reporting, Labour will put people back at the centre of how public money is managed and how monetary policy supports a stable, growing economy.

### Growing the economy and backing those who do the work

New Zealand's economy grows when the people doing the work have the confidence and opportunity to invest, hire and expand.

Labour will create the conditions for people and businesses to succeed: backing investment, helping businesses grow and create jobs, and ensuring the tax system supports investment and productivity.

#### Labour will:

- Invest in productivity and growth through infrastructure, technology, skills, research and development, and practical support for small businesses to grow and create jobs
- Make sure the tax system supports productive investment, including a capital gains tax that helps shift investment away from housing speculation and towards a productive economy that lifts wages and creates jobs
- Create a New Zealand Future Fund to protect our assets, make long-term investments in New Zealand, improve access to capital, and support high-growth businesses, innovation and infrastructure
- Invest in people by providing affordable public services like three free GP visits for all New Zealanders, education, training and transport that help Kiwis participate in the economy and get ahead

The debt burden should not be shouldered by future generations. That is the future cost of failing to invest in the infrastructure and productive capacity we need.

Under Labour, every dollar should work harder and smarter for New Zealanders, funding the services people rely on today while making the investments that grow the economy tomorrow. These investments will help lift productivity, strengthen economic resilience, and ensure more New Zealanders can build their future here.

### Investing in our people, communities and long-term future

Strong public services are part of a strong economy. When families can afford to see a doctor, get a good education, get to work or study on reliable public transport, and get the support they need, it makes life easier. They are healthier, more productive, and can build a better future in New Zealand.

Public services are an investment. The right investment in health, education, housing and social services can prevent problems from becoming more serious and expensive later. Early intervention and the right workforce can reduce pressure on hospitals, police and the justice system, while helping more people stay healthy, in work and independent.

Labour will invest in modernising health, education and other essential services so they are easier to access, more affordable and more productive - making better use of technology, reducing unnecessary administration, and freeing up frontline workers to spend more time doing the jobs they are trained to do.

Where early investment can prevent greater costs later, government should have the confidence to invest upfront. Day-to-day spending must be sustainable, but Labour will also make responsible capital investments in the things New Zealand will rely on for decades, like hospitals, schools and infrastructure. Sometimes borrowing for those investments is the sensible choice that saves money later - failing to invest simply leaves a bigger bill for the future.

The test for every investment is value: does it improve people's lives, strengthen the economy, prevent greater costs in the future, or build assets that future generations will benefit from?

Frequently asked questions
What are Labour's fiscal objectives?
Return to an OBEGAL surplus by 2029/30; reduce net debt to around 20% of GDP; keep core Crown expenditure and revenue at around 33% of GDP in the medium term; and improve transparency by establishing a Parliamentary Budget Office to independently analyse the government's books and every party's election commitments.

When will Labour return the Budget to surplus?
Labour will return the operating balance (OBEGAL) to surplus by 2029/30, the same timing forecast in Budget 2026, while continuing to invest in the people, services and infrastructure New Zealand needs.

What is OBEGAL, and why is Labour changing the measure it uses?
OBEGAL (the operating balance before gains and losses) is the standard measure of the government's day-to-day fiscal position. Labour will return to the original OBEGAL measure, removing OBEGALx, a variant introduced by the current Government that excludes ACC revenue and expenses from the calculation.

What is Labour's net debt target?
Labour aims to reduce net debt to around 20% of GDP. It will use the net debt measure, which accounts for the government's financial assets, such as the Super Fund and advances, as well as its liabilities, including debt held by other Crown agencies like Kainga Ora. This gives governments more room to make productive investments that grow the economy, while still keeping debt under control.

What is a Parliamentary Budget Office?
An independent body Labour will establish to analyse the government's books and cost every political party's policies, giving voters clear, independent information on the true cost of political promises on a consistent, independent basis.

What is wellbeing reporting, and why will Labour restore it?
Wellbeing reporting was a requirement under the Public Finance Act for the government to report on the wellbeing impacts of its fiscal decisions, alongside traditional economic measures. Labour will restore it so that decisions take into account their effect on the lives and livelihoods of New Zealanders, not just headline economic indicators.

What is the Reserve Bank's dual mandate?
A dual mandate directs the Reserve Bank to manage monetary policy with two objectives: keeping prices stable over the medium term, and supporting maximum sustainable employment. Labour will restore this dual mandate, which is also used by central banks in the United States and Australia.

How will Labour grow the economy under this strategy?
- Invest in productivity and growth through infrastructure, technology, skills, research and development, and support for small businesses
- Use the tax system, including a targeted capital gains tax, to shift investment from housing speculation towards a productive economy
- Create a New Zealand Future Fund to make long-term investments and protect Crown assets
- Invest in affordable public services like three free GP visits for all New Zealanders, education, training and transport that help Kiwis participate in the economy and get ahead

What is the New Zealand Future Fund and how does it fit into this strategy?
The New Zealand Future Fund is a proposed fund to protect Crown assets, make long-term investments in New Zealand, improve access to capital, and support high-growth businesses, innovation and infrastructure. It is one of the tools Labour will use to grow the economy within its fiscal objectives, rather than relying only on spending cuts.

Labour will balance the books, back the people doing the work, and invest in the services New Zealanders rely on.

Better today, better tomorrow.

## Fixing the Emissions Trading Scheme

A Labour government will fix the broken Emissions Trading Scheme as an urgent priority, and put New Zealand on course to meet its Paris Agreement targets.

A Labour government will fix the broken Emissions Trading Scheme as an urgent priority.

## Foreign Affairs

Labour will support multilateral institutions, defend peace and international law, and deepen New Zealand's relationships with the EU, Canada, ASEAN and the Pacific.

Key facts
- Multilateral institutions: review and mature the UN Charter, support the World Health Organization and adopt the updated WHO health regulations
- Peace and security: advocate for an ICJ advisory opinion on lethal fully autonomous weapons, establish clear parliamentary scrutiny if New Zealand joins armed conflicts, and strengthen oversight of payloads launched from New Zealand
- Relationships: prioritise the EU and Canada, deepen ties with ASEAN countries, and develop new market opportunities in Africa and South America
- Recognise the State of Palestine, place economic sanctions on Israel, and ensure the NZ Super Fund and ACC divest from holdings on the UN list of companies operating in the occupied territories
- Intervene in support of South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice in respect of a breach of the Genocide Convention
- Overseas development assistance progressively increased towards 0.7% of GNI as fiscal conditions allow
- Human rights: a programme to support human rights defenders, and advocacy for gender apartheid to be recognised in the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty

### Multilateral institutions

Labour will support the development of our multilateral institutions, including reviewing and maturing the UN Charter so it's fit for purpose.

Labour will support the good work of our multilateral organisations such as the World Health Organization and will adopt the updated WHO health regulations.

### Partnerships

Labour will prioritise growing our relationship with the EU and with Canada and exploring options for the development of those relationships in response to the challenges of today's world and in defence of international law, science and our values.

We will deepen our relationship with ASEAN countries, and develop new market opportunities, including in Africa and South America.

### Defending peace

In a world where technology is shifting and removing the offramps toward war, Labour will defend peace.

- We will advocate for an ICJ advisory opinion on the legality of lethal fully autonomous weapons and support international efforts to ban them
- We will establish clear parliamentary scrutiny if New Zealand joins armed conflicts
- We will strengthen oversight of payloads launched from New Zealand to ensure compliance with the current law

### Human rights

Labour will contribute to the development of the law that protects the rights of women and girls and advocate for gender apartheid to be recognised in the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty.

We will support those whose moral courage defies their reality by strengthening New Zealand's advocacy for democracy, peace and human rights, including in Myanmar; and establishing a programme to support human rights defenders, providing a safe haven for those acutely targeted precisely because of their potential to bring about positive change for human rights.

### International law

Labour will intervene in support of South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice in respect of a breach of the Genocide Convention.

Labour will recognise the State of Palestine.

Labour will place economic sanctions on Israel and ensure the NZ Super Fund and ACC divest from holdings on the UN list of companies operating in the occupied territories.

### Climate, development and the Pacific

Labour will re-engage strongly in international climate diplomacy and support the global transition away from fossil fuels. See also Labour's plan to fix the Emissions Trading Scheme.

Labour will progressively increase overseas development assistance towards 0.7% of GNI as fiscal conditions allow.

We will support closer economic integration across the Pacific and make it easier and cheaper to move money and data across the Pacific. Labour will also expand visa-waiver access for citizens of the Pacific Islands Forum nations.

See all of Labour's policies →

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's foreign affairs policy?
Labour will support the development of multilateral institutions, defend peace and international law, strengthen New Zealand's advocacy for democracy and human rights, re-engage in international climate diplomacy, and grow relationships with the EU, Canada, ASEAN countries and the Pacific.

Labour will recognise the State of Palestine.

Labour will place economic sanctions on Israel and ensure the NZ Super Fund and ACC divest from holdings on the UN list of companies operating in the occupied territories. Labour will also intervene in support of South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice in respect of a breach of the Genocide Convention.

What will Labour do on the United Nations and the World Health Organization?
Labour will support the development of multilateral institutions, including reviewing and maturing the UN Charter so it's fit for purpose. Labour will support the good work of multilateral organisations such as the World Health Organization and will adopt the updated WHO health regulations.

Which international relationships will Labour prioritise?
Labour will prioritise growing New Zealand's relationship with the EU and with Canada, and explore options for developing those relationships in response to the challenges of today's world and in defence of international law, science and our values. Labour will also deepen the relationship with ASEAN countries and develop new market opportunities, including in Africa and South America.

What is Labour's position on autonomous weapons?
Labour will advocate for an ICJ advisory opinion on the legality of lethal fully autonomous weapons and support international efforts to ban them.

Will Parliament have a say if New Zealand joins armed conflicts?
Labour will establish clear parliamentary scrutiny if New Zealand joins armed conflicts.

What will Labour do about payloads launched from New Zealand?
Labour will strengthen oversight of payloads launched from New Zealand to ensure compliance with the current law.

What will Labour do for the rights of women and girls internationally?
Labour will contribute to the development of the law that protects the rights of women and girls and advocate for gender apartheid to be recognised in the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty.

How will Labour support human rights defenders?
Labour will strengthen New Zealand's advocacy for democracy, peace and human rights, including in Myanmar, and establish a programme to support human rights defenders, providing a safe haven for those acutely targeted precisely because of their potential to bring about positive change for human rights.

What is Labour's approach to international climate diplomacy?
Labour will re-engage strongly in international climate diplomacy and support the global transition away from fossil fuels.

Will Labour increase overseas development assistance?
Labour will progressively increase overseas development assistance towards 0.7% of GNI as fiscal conditions allow.

What will Labour do in the Pacific?
Labour will support closer economic integration across the Pacific and make it easier and cheaper to move money and data across the Pacific. Labour will also expand visa-waiver access to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations.

How does this relate to Labour's other policies?
Labour's commitment on international climate diplomacy sits alongside its plan to fix the Emissions Trading Scheme and meet Paris Agreement targets. Its Pacific visa-waiver commitment is part of Labour's immigration policy.

New Zealand is at its best when it stands up for open trade, for collective action on climate, for international law, for multilateral institutions, and for peace.

## Freeze Fuel Tax

Labour will freeze fuel excise tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030.

When families are already paying more at the pump, the last thing they need is Christopher Luxon and National reaching into their pockets for more.

Labour will freeze fuel excise tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030.

Higher fuel costs flow through the entire economy. They mean higher costs for farmers, truck drivers, tradies and businesses, and ultimately higher prices for the goods New Zealanders buy.

documents/futurefund.md.title: Labour's New Zealand Future Fund
documents/futurefund.md.text:
## The New Zealand Future Fund

Labour will create an independently governed New Zealand Future Fund to invest in infrastructure and innovative Kiwi businesses.

Key facts
- Purpose: invest in infrastructure and innovative New Zealand businesses to create secure, well-paid jobs
- Seeded with existing Crown-owned assets (commercial and public good purpose) plus an initial capital contribution
- Sits alongside and separate from the NZ Super Fund
- Independently governed by the Guardians of the Super Fund; the Minister of Finance is sole shareholder with no power to direct individual investments
- Seeded assets are protected in law from sale; other assets need explicit Ministerial approval to sell
- Status: the first step in a wider Labour economic plan

### Why a Future Fund, and why now?

Right now, record numbers of Kiwis are leaving. National has no plan to grow the economy or create jobs. Their only answer is to sell off assets and open the door wider to foreign investors, giving away our future instead of building it.

New Zealand has the talent and ideas. What's missing is the backing. Too often, Kiwi businesses are forced overseas or bought out by foreign investors – taking jobs, opportunities, and wealth away with them.

There are 40,000 fewer jobs now than there were when Christopher Luxon became Prime Minister. Every day, more than 200 New Zealanders leave the country in search of opportunities they should find here. New Zealand's economy shrank by nearly a full percent last quarter.

### What other countries have done

Other countries have built wealth by backing their own potential.

Singapore's Temasek began modestly in 1974 with S$354 million - today it is worth more than S$434 billion.

Australia's superannuation has grown to A$4.2 trillion, helping drive investment in its people and industries.

New Zealand's own Super Fund has grown to $85 billion and delivered strong returns, but only 11 percent of it is invested here at home. That's part of the problem: too little of our own capital backs our own ideas.

### How the Future Fund will work

The New Zealand Future Fund will sit alongside, and separate from, the New Zealand Super Fund.

It will be established with a foundation of existing government assets and an initial capital contribution, and will be independently governed by the Guardians of the Super Fund, with the Minister of Finance as sole shareholder.

The Future Fund will be seeded with a small number of Crown-owned assets that have both a commercial and public good purpose, providing a steady revenue stream through dividends and an asset base to leverage. Those seeded assets will be protected in law - they cannot be sold and will remain in public ownership for generations to come. Other assets will require explicit Ministerial approval before being sold.

The Future Fund will operate independently, guided by legislation and a public policy statement. The Minister of Finance will set broad objectives through a letter of expectation, but will have no power to direct individual investments. The Fund will have the authority to invest and borrow.

Returns will be both financial and social - stronger communities, lower costs, more resilient industries, and opportunities that keep talent and ideas in New Zealand. That might include backing community renewable energy or high-tech start-ups.

### Three guiding principles

- Wealth creation with purpose: directing investment to solving real problems: affordable healthcare, warm homes, higher productivity, and a zero-carbon economy.
- Partnership: working alongside business, unions, and communities to shape and create new markets, providing clarity, direction, and confidence to invest for the long term.
- Investing in ourselves: mobilising New Zealand's own savings, skills and innovation to create jobs and opportunity here at home.

### Labour's first-term focus areas

- Make and keep more wealth in New Zealand - invest in productive industries, and create a tax system that rewards work and productive investment over speculation.
- Clean, affordable energy - accelerate new generation and storage and upgrade the grid, so power is cheaper and more reliable.
- Skills and tech adoption - turbo-charge apprenticeships and mid-career upskilling, and help small firms adopt proven technology.
- Faster access to quality, affordable public services - building technological capacity in health, education and local services.
- Modern, resilient infrastructure that connects regions and unlocks growth.

Frequently asked questions
What will the Future Fund invest in?
Infrastructure and innovative Kiwi businesses, plus assets and projects with both a commercial and public good purpose, such as community renewable energy or high-tech start-ups.

How is the Future Fund different from the NZ Super Fund?
It sits alongside and separate from the Super Fund, with its own seeded Crown assets and governance, though it shares the same independent governing body - the Guardians of the Super Fund.

Who controls how the money is invested?
The Guardians of the Super Fund govern it independently. The Minister of Finance is the sole shareholder and sets broad objectives through a letter of expectation, but has no power to direct individual investments.

Can the Future Fund's assets be sold off?
No - assets the Fund is seeded with are protected in law and cannot be sold. Any other assets the Fund holds would require explicit Ministerial approval before being sold.

Is this Labour's full economic plan?
No. Labour says this is the first step, with the rest of its economic plan, covering energy, skills, public services and infrastructure, building on it.

This is how we turn aspiration into action and make New Zealand a place where our kids want to stay and build their lives.

This is how we will build a future made in New Zealand.

documents/good-jobs.md.text:
## Good Jobs

Labour will grow the economy from the ground up - backing tradies, small businesses, graduate nurses and Māori into secure, well-paid work.

Labour's plan for good jobs
- Start Work Now - building homes, fixing schools and repairing hospitals, backing nearly 30,000 apprentices
- Expanding Apprenticeship Boost - a $1,000 toolbox grant and five new trades from 1 July 2027
- Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee - every eligible graduate nurse offered a job from 2027
- Pay Equity - a $4 an hour pay rise for care and support workers from 2027
- Small Business Action Plan - a 15-day payment rule and a $10,000 instant write-off
- Small Business First - a 15% target for government contracts to go to small business
- Backing Māori into Skilled Work - $21 million a year in Māori-led training

### Why it matters

Christopher Luxon promised to fix the economy. For many New Zealanders, it's gotten worse.

171,000people are out of work under National

20,000people have lost their jobs in construction

~2,000People leaving New Zealand every week

54Nurses added to public hospitals in two years

## Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee

How it works Why it matters Eligibility Nurses by region Funding FAQs
Labour will offer every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse a job in our health system.

Key facts
- Every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse will be offered a job in the health system
- Around 2,400 nurses graduates every year will get a job offer
- Roles will be offered on graduation rather than staggered throughout the year, starting in 2027, and will be at least 0.8 FTE
- Graduate nurses will be offered jobs through the existing Advanced Choice of Employment (ACE) and primary care employment schemes
- Registered and enrolled nurses are eligible
- Double funding for graduate nursing roles in primary and community healthcare
- Costed at $525 million. Funded from the Budget's Vote Health cost-pressure funding

If you train as a nurse here and qualify, there will be a place for you here under a Labour Government.

### How it works

- Every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse will be offered a role through the existing Advanced Choice of Employment (ACE) and primary care employment schemes.
- Jobs will be offered at graduation, rather than staggered throughout the year, and will be for at least 0.8 full-time equivalent (FTE).
- The policy means all of the estimated 2,400 nurses who graduate a year will get a job offer. Both registered and enrolled nurses are eligible.
- Labour will double funding for graduate nursing roles in primary and community healthcare.

### Why it matters

New Zealand needs more nurses in our hospitals, primary care, aged care, community services and rural areas.

But under National, we're training nurses here only for too many of them to find there's no job for them after they graduate.

National has made it harder to hire the nurses our hospitals need. They've had a hiring freeze in place, and in two years, just 54 nurses have been added to the public health system.

In 2025, fewer than half of graduating nurses were initially offered jobs through the ACE programme. Some waited months for an offer, while others were offered less than 0.8 FTE.

When hospitals can't hire the nurses they need, there are fewer nurses on the ward, more pressure on the staff who are there, and patients wait longer for care.

Nurses who have been trained in New Zealand, and want to work in our communities, have no other option but to look overseas for work.

We can't afford another three years of National holding our health system back.

### A smart investment

Backing graduate nurses means more nurses caring for patients, less pressure on existing staff, and a better start for people beginning their careers.

The Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee means all of the estimated 2,400 nurses who graduate a year will get a job offer.

It will apply to graduates sitting their State Final examination from July 2026 onwards. From 2027, eligible graduates will be offered roles on graduation.

### Eligibility and cost

Job offers will depend on graduates passing their State Final examination and required pre-employment checks.

Graduates must also be a New Zealand citizen, permanent resident, returning resident visa holder or Australian citizen, and have completed their nursing qualification at a New Zealand tertiary institution.

The cost of the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee is $525 million. It will be funded from health cost-pressure funding.

### Nursing numbers under National, by district

Under National, recruitment has been restricted across the country. In some areas, including Auckland and Counties Manukau, the number of nurses has actually fallen. Jobs under the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee will be available across New Zealand, in hospitals, primary care and community healthcare, helping fill these gaps.

Frequently asked questions
How many nurses will this add?
Around 2,400 nurses graduate in New Zealand every year, and Labour will ensure every eligible graduate gets a job offer. Both registered and enrolled nurses are eligible.

When will the guarantee apply from?
It will apply to graduates sitting their State Final examination from July 2026 onwards. Eligible graduates will be offered a job in a hospital, primary care or community healthcare setting. From 2027, roles will be offered on graduation rather than staggered throughout the year.

Who is eligible?
The policy applies to graduates who sit their State Final examination from July 2026 onwards and complete a pre-registration nursing qualification approved by the Nursing Council of New Zealand.

Job offers will depend on graduates passing their State Final examination and all required pre-employment checks. They must also:

- Be a New Zealand citizen, New Zealand permanent resident or returning resident visa holder, or an Australian citizen
- Have studied their qualification in New Zealand at a New Zealand tertiary institution

Why are you doing this?
New Zealand needs more nurses. But right now, we are training nurses here only for too many of them to find there is no job for them after they graduate.

National has made it harder to hire the nurses our hospitals need. They've had a hiring freeze in place, and in two years, just 54 nurses have been added to the public health system.

In 2025, fewer than half of graduating nurses were initially offered jobs through the ACE programme. Some waited months for an offer, while others were offered less than 0.8 FTE. That leaves graduate nurses out of work or looking overseas at the same time our health system needs them.

Labour will back our graduate nurses to find a job here at home.

Where will the jobs be?
Jobs will be available across New Zealand in hospitals, primary care and community healthcare. Under National, recruitment has been restricted across the country - in some areas, including Auckland and Counties Manukau, the number of nurses has actually fallen. Labour will make sure graduate nurses can move from training into work, while helping fill the gaps across our health system.

What will it cost and how will you pay for it?
The Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee will cost $525 million. It will be funded from Vote Health cost-pressure funding.

More nurses caring for patients, and a job here at home for the nurses we train.

Backing our graduate nurses to find a job here at home.

documents/immigration.md.text:
## Immigration

Labour will plan immigration around New Zealand's capacity, protect migrants from exploitation and make it easier for Pacific whānau to reconnect.

Key facts
- Immigration planned around capacity through a Government Policy Statement that reflects workforce demographic, housing and infrastructure needs
- Permanent residence after four years in New Zealand instead of two, supported by orientation and civic education delivered by community education providers
- Protection from exploitation: migrants can move between accredited employers after three months, and the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme is strengthened
- Humanitarian appeals against deportation protected, and a citizenship pathway for children born in New Zealand
- Reviews of parent visa, health and English-language rules
- Pacific visa-waiver access expanded to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations

### Plan immigration around New Zealand's capacity

Labour will plan immigration around New Zealand's capacity by setting goals through a Government Policy Statement on immigration that reflects our workforce demographic, housing and infrastructure needs.

### Encourage migrants to put down roots

Labour will encourage migrants to put down roots by extending the period migrants must live here before becoming eligible for permanent residence from two years to four.

This will be supported by a programme of New Zealand orientation and civic education delivered by community education providers to strengthen social cohesion.

### Protect migrants from exploitation

Labour will protect migrants from exploitation by:

- Enabling migrants to move between accredited employers after three months
- Strengthening the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme
- Improving access to support in their communities

See also Labour's Fairer Workplaces policy.

### Treat people with decency

Labour will treat people with decency by:

- Protecting humanitarian appeals against deportation
- Setting up a citizenship pathway for children born in New Zealand
- Reviewing parent visa, health and English-language rules

| Area | Labour will |
| --- | --- |
| Permanent residence | Extend the period migrants must live here before becoming eligible from two years to four |
| Changing employers | Enable migrants to move between accredited employers after three months |
| Deportation | Protect humanitarian appeals against deportation |
| Citizenship | Set up a citizenship pathway for children born in New Zealand |
| Visa rules | Review parent visa, health and English-language rules |

### Pacific visa-waiver

Labour will expand visa-waiver access to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations, making it easier and more affordable for Pacific whānau to reconnect.

We know that too often, it will fall on families here in New Zealand to sponsor loved ones from the islands for a visit.

Families shouldn't have to choose between meeting their everyday costs and being able to welcome loved ones from the islands to New Zealand.

We recognise New Zealand's special relationship and deep family ties with Pacific countries, and we hope this will bring relief to Pacific families welcoming their loved ones from the islands to our beautiful country.

Read about Labour's wider plans for the Pacific in Foreign Affairs →

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's immigration policy?
Labour will plan immigration around New Zealand's capacity, encourage migrants to put down roots, protect migrants from exploitation and treat people with decency. Labour will also expand visa-waiver access to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations.

How will Labour plan immigration around New Zealand's capacity?
Labour will plan immigration around New Zealand's capacity by setting goals through a Government Policy Statement on immigration that reflects the workforce demographic, housing and infrastructure needs.

How long will migrants have to live in New Zealand before they can get permanent residence?
Labour will extend the period migrants must live in New Zealand before becoming eligible for permanent residence from two years to four. This will be supported by a programme of New Zealand orientation and civic education delivered by community education providers to strengthen social cohesion.

How will Labour protect migrants from exploitation?
Labour will enable migrants to move between accredited employers after three months, strengthen the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme, and improve access to support in their communities.

What will Labour do about deportation and citizenship for children born in New Zealand?
Labour will protect humanitarian appeals against deportation and set up a citizenship pathway for children born in New Zealand.

What will Labour review in parent visa, health and English-language rules?
Labour will review parent visa, health and English-language rules as part of treating people with decency.

What is Labour's Pacific visa-waiver policy?
Labour will expand visa-waiver access to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations, making it easier and more affordable for Pacific whānau to reconnect.

Why is Labour expanding visa-waiver access for the Pacific?
Too often, it falls on families in New Zealand to sponsor loved ones from the islands for a visit. Families shouldn't have to choose between meeting their everyday costs and being able to welcome loved ones from the islands to New Zealand. Labour recognises New Zealand's special relationship and deep family ties with Pacific countries.

How does Labour's immigration policy relate to its other policies?
Protecting migrants from exploitation sits alongside Labour's Fairer Workplaces policy. The Pacific visa-waiver is also part of the Pacific commitments in Labour's Foreign Affairs policy.

Labour will back people to build their lives and careers here, while ensuring immigration supports the long-term interests of New Zealand.

Better starts now.

documents/kids-off-screens.md.title: Keeping Kids off Screens
documents/kids-off-screens.md.text:
## Keeping Kids off Screens

Screens and childhood More sport, play and fun The right screen at the right time Support for parents FAQs
Labour will back more sport and play, set clearer rules on screen use in schools, and support parents to keep kids safe online.

Key facts
- Three ways to keep kids off screens for longer: more sport and play, the right screen at the right time, and support for parents
- Active Me - Kia Tū kept going. $3 million a year for another four years, with grants of up to $300 a year for two years towards registration, uniforms and equipment
- An extra $4 million a year through Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa, ring-fenced for community groups running after-school sport and activities
- Clearer national advice on screen use for early childhood education and schools, with guidance for different ages
- Schools and kura must have clear screen-use policies, plus clearer expectations for safe settings and appropriate content on school devices
- The existing ban on mobile phones in schools stays
- Online-safety tools made easier to find and use, including the free Switch on Safety filter and the Digital Guardian Guide

Three ways we'll keep kids off screens for longer:

- More sport. More play. More fun. Help cover sport costs with grants of up to $300 a year for two years, and invest $4 million more each year in after-school activities.
- The right screen at the right time. Set clearer national expectations and require schools to have sensible policies on screen use.
- Support for parents. Make online-safety tools easier to find and use, and help schools use new technology safely.

We cannot expect parents to solve this on their own. Clearer rules must go hand in hand with better alternatives for children.

### Screens are taking up more of childhood

Smart devices can have real benefits. But social media companies are reaching children younger and younger and taking up a significant part of their day. Parents need support, and kids need time away from a screen.

90%of teenagers reported using social media

62%started using social media aged 10 to 13

2.5hrsaverage social media use a day

32%of teenagers spend at least five hours a day on social media

Source: Public Health Communication Centre Aotearoa.

### 1. More sport. More play. More fun.

If we want children to spend less time on screens, we have to give them the chance to do something else. And those opportunities need to be affordable.

Sport, play and recreation help kids make friends, discover new interests and build confidence. But costs add up. Registration fees. Uniforms. Boots. Equipment. When household budgets are stretched, sport and after-school activities can be the things families have to cut back on.

| Programme | What Labour will do | Funding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active Me - Kia Tū | Keep the programme going, with grants of up to $300 a year for two years towards registration, uniforms and equipment | $3 million a year, for another four years |
| Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa | Ring-fenced funding for community groups running after-school sport and activities for kids | An additional $4 million a year |

#### Help with fees, uniforms and equipment

Labour will provide $3 million a year to keep Active Me - Kia Tū going. It offers grants of up to $300 a year for two years to help children take part in sport and recreation, covering costs such as registration, uniforms and equipment.

More than 10,000 children have benefited since 2021. With existing funding due to expire in 2026, Labour will give the programme certainty for another four years.

#### More opportunities after school

Labour will invest an additional $4 million a year through Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa, which will be ring-fenced specifically for community groups running after-school sport and activities for kids.

Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa helps local clubs and organisations deliver play, recreation and sport for five to 18-year-olds. From 2020 to 2024, it supported 5,281 projects and nearly two million opportunities for young people to take part.

This isn't just about less screen time. These are practical ways to make sure there are more chances to join in, have fun and be a kid.

### 2. The right screen at the right time

Technology has a place in education. Used well, it can support learning and give teachers useful tools. But not every lesson needs a device.

Children also need to read, write, chat, move around, solve problems and learn alongside each other. Parents should know screens are used at school because they help children learn, not simply because they are there.

#### Clear national advice

Labour will work with educators, health experts and young people to update Ministry of Education recommendations for screen use in early childhood education and schools, with clearer guidance for different ages.

#### Policies schools must have

We will change education regulations so school and kura boards are required to put clear screen-use policies in place, including when and how devices are used in the classroom.

We will also set clearer expectations for safe settings and appropriate content on school devices.

#### Keep phones out of the school day

We will retain the existing ban on mobile phones in schools, so children can concentrate on their learning, friendships and the school day.

### 3. Back parents to keep kids safe

Parents know their children best. But apps and online risks change quickly, and even parents who set clear boundaries can struggle to keep up. They need practical help, not another lecture.

#### Help parents make informed choices

Labour will make existing online-safety tools easier to find and use. That includes the free Switch on Safety filter and the Digital Guardian Guide, which help families make decisions about devices, online content and safer use at home.

#### Help schools use technology safely

We have already announced an AI in Education team to support schools, teachers and students (see Labour's AI Action Plan). We will also work with experts and young people on an education AI app designed to support learning in a safer environment.

Together with clearer expectations for school devices, these steps will help children benefit from new technology without being left to navigate the risks on their own.

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's Keeping Kids off Screens policy?
Keeping Kids off Screens is Labour's plan to help kids be kids for longer, in three ways:

- More sport, play and after-school activities, with help towards the costs
- Clearer national expectations and sensible screen-use policies in schools
- Practical support for parents, including online-safety tools that are easier to find and use.

Why is Labour doing this?
Smart devices can have real benefits, but social media companies are reaching children younger and younger and taking up a significant part of their day. Parents need support, and kids need time away from a screen.

How much time do teenagers spend on social media?
Figures from the Public Health Communication Centre Aotearoa show that 90% of teenagers reported using social media, 62% started using social media aged 10 to 13, average use is 2.5 hours a day, and 32% of teenagers spend at least five hours a day on social media.

What is Active Me - Kia Tū and what will Labour do?
Active Me - Kia Tū offers grants of up to $300 a year for two years to help children take part in sport and recreation, covering costs such as registration, uniforms and equipment. More than 10,000 children have benefited since 2021. With existing funding due to expire in 2026, Labour will provide $3 million a year to keep the programme going, giving it certainty for another four years.

What is Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa and what is the extra $4 million for?
Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa helps local clubs and organisations deliver play, recreation and sport for five to 18-year-olds. From 2020 to 2024 it supported 5,281 projects and nearly two million opportunities for young people to take part. Labour will invest an additional $4 million a year through the programme, ring-fenced specifically for community groups running after-school sport and activities for kids.

What will change in schools?
- Labour will work with educators, health experts and young people to update Ministry of Education recommendations for screen use in early childhood education and schools, with clearer guidance for different ages
- Education regulations will change so school and kura boards are required to put clear screen-use policies in place, including when and how devices are used in the classroom
- Labour will set clearer expectations for safe settings and appropriate content on school devices

Will the ban on mobile phones in schools stay?
Yes. Labour will retain the existing ban on mobile phones in schools, so children can concentrate on their learning, friendships and the school day.

How will Labour support parents?
Labour will make existing online-safety tools easier to find and use, including the free Switch on Safety filter and the Digital Guardian Guide, which help families make decisions about devices, online content and safer use at home.

Labour has also announced an AI in Education team to support schools, teachers and students, and will work with experts and young people on an education AI app designed to support learning in a safer environment.

Is Labour telling parents how to manage screen time?
No. Government should not be making decisions about a child's screen time, but it can back parents, set sensible rules and give kids better things to do beyond a screen.

How much will this cost?
Labour will provide $3 million a year to keep Active Me - Kia Tū going for another four years, and invest an additional $4 million a year through Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa for after-school sport and activities.

This is how we help kids be kids for longer.

Better starts now.

documents/maori-trades-training.md.text:
## Backing Māori into Skilled Work

Why it matters How it works Industries covered Funding FAQs
Labour will invest $21 million a year in Māori-led training that helps more whānau Māori gain skills and move into good, well-paid work.

Key facts
- By Māori, for Māori. Māori providers backed to design and deliver training that works for their communities and local employers
- Skills that lead to jobs. Practical training linked to real jobs and recognised qualifications
- Earn and get ahead. Helping people move into secure, paid work and gain skills that lead to better pay
- Support to succeed. Mentoring and practical support to complete training, get into work and stay in work
- Open to Māori of all ages - for people looking for a way into work, wanting to retrain, or wanting a better job
- Costed at $21 million a year, funded through reprioritisation and existing baselines in Budget 2027

Labour will support more whānau Māori to gain skills, get into secure work and build a better future.

Labour will back kaupapa Māori training delivered by marae, iwi trusts and Māori providers, working with local employers to connect people with real jobs. Training will combine practical skills with mentoring and support, helping people get into work, stay in work and gain qualifications that help them get ahead.

### Why it matters

Labour will build a country where everyone who works hard has the chance to get ahead. Right now, too many Māori are missing out on the opportunity that comes with good, well-paid, skilled work.

Māori unemployment is more than double the national rate. More than one in ten Māori are unemployed, and around one in five rangatahi Māori aged 15 to 24 are not in work, education, or training.

Under the current Government, around 40,000 more people are unemployed nationally, and an estimated 2,000 people are leaving New Zealand every week.

There is a better way. Marae, iwi and Māori providers know their people and their communities. They know the local employers who need workers, and they know what support people need to succeed. Labour will back them to help more Māori gain skills and move into good jobs.

When people get the right training and support, they can get into work, earn more and build a future for themselves and their whānau.

### How it works

Māori providers will be backed to deliver training that leads to work.

- By Māori, for Māori. Māori providers will design and deliver training that works for their communities and local employers.
- Skills that lead to jobs. Practical training linked to real jobs and qualifications.
- Earn and get ahead. Helping people move into secure, paid work and gain skills that can lead to better pay.
- Support to succeed. Mentoring and practical support to help people complete their training, get into work and stay in work.
- Open to Māori of all ages. For people looking for a way into work, wanting to retrain, or wanting a better job.

Providers will be able to apply for funding through a contestable fund to design and deliver programmes around the skills local employers need.

### A smart investment in people

Backing Māori to gain skills and get into good work is good for whānau, good for businesses, and good for New Zealand.

We know Māori-led trades training works. An earlier programme under the previous Labour Government helped people move from unemployment, casual work and lower-skilled jobs into more secure, skilled work. It also helped people gain industry qualifications.

The benefits went beyond a pay packet. More than 80 percent of participants said the programme helped them better manage their health and wellbeing, while more than 90 percent said it had a positive impact on their whānau.

Of the 2,978 people who took part in the previous programme before it was cut, 72 percent were in work by September 2024, and nearly three-quarters of those were in permanent jobs.

### Which industries will be covered

A wide range of industries will be covered, based on where people are needed. Under the previous programme, construction was the largest sector, followed by agriculture, forestry and fishing, and healthcare and social assistance. Labour's plan will connect training opportunities with real jobs in local communities.

The next Labour Government will build on that success so more Māori get the opportunity to get ahead. Every person who gains skills, gets a good job, and earns more can build a stronger future for themselves and their whānau, and New Zealand gets more of the skilled people it needs.

### Investing in the future

Labour will establish a contestable, grant-based fund for Māori providers to design and deliver employment-focused training programmes.

The programme is fully costed at $21 million a year. It will be funded through reprioritisation and existing baselines in Budget 2027, and will start soon after that. Māori providers already have experience delivering this kind of training, so support can move quickly to communities and people into training.

Frequently asked questions
How does the programme work?
Labour will invest in Māori-led training that helps people gain skills and move into good work. Māori providers will be backed to deliver practical training linked to real jobs, with mentoring and support to help people complete their training, get into work and stay in work. The focus is skills that lead to jobs, better pay, and a stronger future for whānau.

Why is Labour doing this?
Too many Māori are missing out on the security and opportunities that come with good work. Māori unemployment is more than double the national rate. We also know this approach works: of the 2,978 people who took part in the previous programme that National cut, 72 percent were in work by September 2024, and nearly three-quarters of those were in permanent jobs. Labour will build on what works and back more Māori into skilled, secure work.

Which trades are covered?
A wide range of industries will be covered, based on where people are needed. Under the previous programme, construction was the largest sector, followed by agriculture, forestry and fishing, and healthcare and social assistance. Labour's plan will connect training opportunities with real jobs in local communities.

When will it start?
The programme will be running as soon as possible after Budget 2027. Māori providers already have experience delivering this kind of training, so support can move quickly to communities and people into training.

Who will benefit, and how many?
The programme will be open to Māori of all ages, focused on people who need a pathway into work, want to retrain, or need extra support to get into a secure job and stay there. The previous programme attracted more applications than could be funded, showing strong demand.

How much will it cost, and how have you worked it out?
Labour has costed the programme at $21 million a year, based on the cost of delivering the previous programme. It will be paid for through existing government funding and reprioritisation.

This is a practical investment in people, helping more Māori gain skills, earn more and build a future here at home.

Backing Māori to learn, earn and build a future here at home.

documents/maternityscans.md.title: Labour's Free Maternity Scans with the Medicard
documents/maternityscans.md.text:
## Free Maternity Scans With the Medicard

From July 2028, Labour will make maternity scans free everywhere in New Zealand with the Medicard.

Key facts
- Every referred maternity scan is free, everywhere in New Zealand, from July 2028
- Scans currently cost up to $90 each, and are only free already in some regions (Tairāwhiti, Nelson and the West Coast)
- Cost: $28.6 million a year, funded by Labour's simple, targeted capital gains tax
- 24 paid trainee sonographer positions funded to grow the workforce, costing less than $3 million a year
- Entitlement loaded automatically onto the Medicard after a referral from a GP, midwife or specialist
- Sits alongside the Medicard's three free doctor's visits a year and free cervical screening

### How it works

Labour will fund every scan a doctor, midwife or specialist refers a pregnant woman for. After the referral, the entitlement is loaded onto her Medicard.

No forms, no invoices. All a new mum will need is her Medicard, or the Medicard app on her phone.

### How much this saves families

A woman having the two routine scans recommended in a straightforward pregnancy, at $90 each, currently pays $180. A woman needing five scans could currently pay up to $450 across her pregnancy. Under Labour, she pays nothing.

### Why this matters

You shouldn't have to worry about money to know you or your baby are okay. Right now, a pregnancy scan can cost up to $90, depending on where you live, and scans are currently only free in some places, like Tairāwhiti, Nelson and the West Coast. Labour will make them free everywhere.

No mum will skip a scan because she can't afford it, helping to look after her and her baby, and easing the pressure on hospitals.

Frequently asked questions
How is it paid for?
Free maternity scans will cost $28.6 million a year, funded by a simple, targeted capital gains tax on profits from the sale of commercial and residential investment property (excluding the family home, farms, businesses, inheritance, and KiwiSaver). Every dollar raised by the CGT is ring-fenced for health, including three free doctor's visits for every New Zealander.

When will it be implemented?
Free scans will be available from July 2028.

Do we have enough sonographers to meet demand?
Labour will grow the workforce by funding 24 paid trainee sonographer positions at Health New Zealand, costing less than $3 million a year from Health NZ baselines.

Who will be entitled to free maternity scans?
Anyone who is pregnant and eligible for publicly funded health services. For a scan to be covered, a referral from a GP, midwife or specialist will be required.

How much money will this save families?
Anyone having the two routine scans recommended in a straightforward pregnancy, at $90 each, saves $180. A woman needing five scans could currently pay up to $450 across her pregnancy. Under Labour, she pays nothing.

Aren't scans already free?
Not everywhere. Scans are currently free in places like Tairāwhiti, Nelson and the West Coast. Under Labour, free scans will be free no matter where you live.

Free maternity scans. Three free doctor's visits. Free cervical screening - all on one Medicard.

Money back in your pocket and just one of the ways Labour policies will make your life better.
