documents/medicard.md.title: Labour's Free Doctor’s Visits with the Medicard
documents/medicard.md.text:
## Free Doctor's Visits with the Medicard

Under Labour, every New Zealander will get three free doctor's visits a year through the new Medicard, paid for by a simple, targeted tax on profit from the sale of investment property.

Key facts
- 3 free doctor's visits a year for every New Zealander, via a new Medicard
- Funded by a 28% tax on the profit made after 1 July 2027 when a commercial or residential property is sold (excluding the family home and farms)
- No tax on any gain made before 1 July 2027
- Full exemptions: the family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances and personal items
- An estimated 9 in 10 New Zealanders won't pay the tax
- Most Kiwis see their GP about 2.5 times a year: from July 2028, an estimated 4 in 5 New Zealanders won't have to pay for a routine GP visit
- A practical plan to free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments every year to make it easier to see a doctor
- Total cost: $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place

### Why Labour is doing this

Labour will ensure New Zealand has a strong, growing economy that rewards hard work and pays for the services we all rely on, like healthcare.

Too much of our national wealth is tied up in property instead of more productive parts of the economy that lift wages and drive innovation. It's one of the reasons New Zealand is falling behind. Labour will change that.

New Zealand cannot realise its potential, create jobs, or deliver the services we all deserve through property investment alone. Our targeted capital gains tax will level the playing field for Kiwi businesses and innovation - helping grow wealth and create jobs.

“I can't afford to go [to the GP] when I really need to. I have to put it on the backburner so that I can afford my rent.”

### The cost of not acting

No one should have to choose between seeing a doctor and putting food on the table, but that's the reality for far too many New Zealanders. Under Christopher Luxon, one in six New Zealanders cannot afford to visit their doctor when they are sick. Some general practice fees are heading towards $100 a visit. It doesn't have to be this way.

“I don't go to the doctor unless really urgent – I'd rather go straight to the hospital. It costs me $54 out of the little money I have left for food.”

### How the Medicard works

Every New Zealander will get a new Medicard that they can use to access three free doctor's visits each year at their enrolled practice. The three free visits are also accessible through a secure app.

- People receive their Medicard at birth, or when they become a citizen, resident, or otherwise eligible for healthcare.
- Your Medicard can be used at the general practice you're enrolled with whenever you need an appointment with a doctor or a nurse.
- The three free visits apply per year and don't roll over if they aren't used within the year, they won't carry into the next.
- Your three free visits cover appointments with a doctor or nurse at your enrolled general practice. They don't include services that are already free (such as immunisations or Access and Choice services), after-hours care, or ACC visits.
- Using a clinical phone triage service will not count toward your three free visits.
- The card-and-app system tracks entitlements in real time, integrates securely with primary and community provider software, and is designed to protect privacy, ensure accessibility (including for non-digital users), and offer multilingual support.
- The Medicard will integrate with My Health Account, New Zealand's digital health identity system, and will hold your National Health Index (NHI) number and health entitlement information.

### How it's funded: the targeted capital gains tax

Labour will introduce a simple, targeted 28% tax on the profit made after 1 July 2027 when a commercial property or residential property (excluding the family home) is sold. Any gain from before that date won't be taxed. Every dollar raised will go directly to our health system.

- It only applies to the profit when a commercial or residential property is sold, excluding the family home.
- Our targeted capital gains tax completely exempts the family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, and any other personal items.
- The tax rate will be 28%, the same as the company tax rate, meaning property profits will be taxed like other business activity.
- No one will pay a single dollar on any gain made before 1 July 2027.

For full worked examples and frequently asked questions on the tax itself, see Labour's capital gains tax policy page.

### Fixing the general practice funding problem

For more than two decades, general practice has been funded mainly by a flat payment for each enrolled person, with clinics allowed to charge a patient co-payment on top. That model is broken: independent analysis in 2022 found general practice was underfunded by around 7.6 percent - about $137 million against total practice income of $1.67 billion.

As part of delivering three free doctor's visits, Labour is proposing a new model known as independent pricing. An Independent Pricing Authority would be up and running by July 2028 and will set an evidence-based national rate for GP funding that reflects real costs and patient need. When the rate goes up, Health NZ will be required to fund the increase the following year - ending the cycle where practices either absorb rising costs or pass them on to patients.

Modelled on Australia's Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority, the body will use comprehensive data to set sustainable prices, including practice costs, staffing, patient mix, service delivery, and sector-wide cost studies. Money currently in co-payments will be added to general practice funding, so clinics won't be worse off under the new system.

### How Labour will free up 4.5 million GP appointments a year

Labour has worked with health experts on a practical plan to free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments every year through simple, affordable changes that free up doctors' time so they can focus on patients, not paperwork.

Simple, affordable changes that free up doctors' time so they can focus on patients.

| Change | Appointments freed up per year |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical phone triage, directing patients to the right care | ~1.9 million (plus a further 2.9 million visits streamlined) |
| Expanding the use of technology to reduce administration | ~1.5 million |
| Support for advice on long-term conditions | ~1 million |
| Targeted funding to expand clinic space in high-demand areas | ~180,000 |

Where a patient's issue is resolved through telehealth triage, it will not count against their annual entitlement to three free doctor's visits.

#### Other changes in the plan

- A new Digital Innovation Fund, so clinics can quickly trial and adopt the best new technology as it becomes available.
- More open and efficient procurement for doctors, including access to the national Health System Catalogue, to reduce everyday running costs.
- A review of telehealth funding to ensure it complements, not replaces, face-to-face care.

### The cost of Labour's plan

Spending ramps up as the Medicard and supporting initiatives roll out, reaching a stable annual cost from 2029/30 onwards.

| Initiative | 2027/28 | 2028/29 | 2029/30 | 2030 & outyears |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free doctor's visits | 323 | 490 | 490 | 490 |
| Medicard and app | 20 | 14 | 14 | 14 |
| Clinical triage | 30 | 30 | 30 | 30 |
| AI scribe technology / Digital Innovation Fund | 4.3 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| Improving self-care | 5 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| Independent Pricing Authority | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 |
| Facilities (grants) | 5 | 5 | 5 | - |
| Total | 393.3 | 553 | 553 | 548 |

Note: The above figures are NZ$ millions

Frequently asked questions
Who has to pay the new property tax?
Only people who sell a commercial property, or a residential property other than their family home, for a profit made after 1 July 2027. Nine out of 10 New Zealanders do not own more than one property or a commercial property, so they won't pay it.

What's exempt from the tax?
The family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances and personal items.

When does the tax start?
It applies only to profit made after 1 July 2027. No gain made before that date is taxed.

How many free doctor's visits will I get, and do they roll over?
Three a year, for every New Zealander, through the new Medicard. They don't roll over if you don't use them within the year, they don't carry into the next.

What's not covered by my three free visits?
Services that are already free, such as immunisations or Access and Choice services, plus after-hours care and ACC visits, are not covered by your three free visits.

What is the Independent Pricing Authority?
A proposed new body, modelled on Australia's Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority, that would set an evidence-based national funding rate for general practice based on real costs and patient need, due to be up and running by July 2028.

Labour will ensure New Zealand is a country that backs its people and its own potential - a place where our kids want to stay and build their lives.

That's what's possible: a strong economy and free doctor's visits for everyone.

documents/pay-equity.md.text:
## Pay Equity

Labour will restore pay equity legislation in its first 100 days and give an immediate pay rise to care and support workers.

Key facts
- Pay equity legislation restored in Labour's first 100 days
- $4 an hour immediate pay rise for care and support workers, from 1 January 2027
- Covers an estimated 65,000 care and support workers
- Worth around $8,320 a year, or $160 a week before tax, for an average full-time worker
- Fully funded within Labour's Fiscal Plan

Care and support workers do some of the most important work in our communities, and overwhelmingly they are women. This immediate pay rise is real money for people who are paying the mortgage, the rent, the power bill and the grocery shop.

An estimated 11,000 New Zealand children are currently in poverty because of National's cancelled pay equity claims. Labour says work should not be undervalued simply because it is work traditionally done by women.

### How it will work

Labour will reinstate pay equity legislation in its first 100 days in office. The reinstated legislation will accommodate the previous work already underway, so women aren't starting their claims from scratch.

From 1 January 2027, care and support workers will receive an immediate pay rise of $4 an hour, worth around $8,320 a year, or $160 a week before tax, for an average full-time worker.

Future pay equity settlements are different. Pay equity is determined through negotiation, and announcing in advance how much has been set aside for individual claims would undermine that process. Future settlements will be funded responsibly through future Budgets as agreements are reached and their costs become clear.

### Part of Labour's Fiscal Plan

The cost of the immediate pay rise for care and support workers is fully funded within Labour's Fiscal Plan, alongside every other election commitment Labour has made.

Frequently asked questions
When will pay equity legislation be restored?
Labour will restore pay equity legislation in its first 100 days in office. The reinstated legislation will accommodate the previous work already underway, so women aren't starting their claims from scratch.

How much will care and support workers' pay increase by?
From 1 January 2027, care and support workers will receive an immediate pay rise of $4 an hour. For the average full-time worker, this means being $8,320 a year better off, or $160 a week before tax.

Who is eligible for the immediate pay rise?
The immediate $4 an hour pay rise applies to care and support workers, the large majority of whom are women.

Will other pay equity claims also be settled immediately?
No. Pay equity is determined through negotiation, and Labour says announcing in advance how much has been set aside for individual claims would undermine that process. Future pay equity settlements will be funded responsibly through future Budgets as agreements are reached and their costs become clear.

How is this policy funded?
The cost of the immediate pay rise for care and support workers is fully funded within Labour's Fiscal Plan.

Why is Labour doing this?
Care and support workers do some of the most important work in communities, and are overwhelmingly women. Labour says National's cancelled pay equity claims have contributed to hardship for women and families, and that work should not be undervalued simply because it is traditionally done by women.

While National takes money out of women's pockets, Labour will put more of it back.

Better starts now.

Labour's 2026 General Election policies for New Zealand will manage the economy responsibly, make healthcare more affordable, cut the cost of getting around, and deliver real action on the cost of living.

Every policy below is fully costed and funded. Click any policy to read the detail, including who is eligible, when it starts and how it is paid for.

### Free Doctor's Visits

### Free Prescriptions

### Frequently asked questions about Labour's 2026 policies

What are Labour's policies for the 2026 New Zealand general election?
Labour's 2026 election policies focus on the things that matter most for everyday New Zealanders including cost-of-living relief, affordable healthcare, and good:

- Cost of living plan: a $20 weekly public transport fare cap, a three-year fuel tax freeze, banning price gouging, fairer grocery prices, the Fair Go Law, cutting student debt, SolarSaver and more
- Affordable healthcare plan: three free GP visits a year through a new Medicard, free prescriptions, free maternity scans, free cervical screening, the ED Recovery Plan, the Family Doctor Loan Scheme and the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee, funded by a targeted capital gains tax
- Good jobs plan: Apprenticeship Boost, Start Work Now, Backing Māori into Skilled Work, the Small Business Action Plan, Small Business First and Fairer Workplaces

Labour has also announced our Fiscal Plan, the New Zealand Future Fund, a targeted capital gains tax on investment property profits, Strengthening KiwiSaver, an AI Action Plan, Safer Online, Keeping Kids off Screens, Pay Equity for Carers and Support Workers and policies on foreign affairs, immigration, disability, and early childhood education.

What is Labour's cost of living plan?
Labour's cost of living plan is a package of practical steps to cut everyday costs. It includes:

- a $20 weekly public transport fare cap in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch and $10 everywhere else, in place by 1 July 2027
- freezing fuel tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030
- three free GP visits a year (Medicard) and free prescriptions
- SolarSaver, removing the upfront cost of solar
- cutting 10% off eligible student loan balances
- banning price gouging and taking on the supermarket giants with fairer grocery prices
- the Fair Go Law banning hidden fees, junk insurance and exit traps
- A Fair Go For Drivers, Banking for Everyone, A Better Deal When You Fly and Cutting Back-to-School Costs

How much will I save under Labour?
You can use the LabourSaver calculator to work out how much your household will save. Savings depend on your household and which policies apply to you:

- three free GP visits a year through the Medicard, saving the average household around $360 a year
- freezing fuel tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030
- free prescriptions, removing the $5 prescription fee
- a $20 weekly cap on public transport fares ($10 outside Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch)
- a $4 an hour pay rise for care and support workers under Pay Equity, worth around $8,320 a year to an average full-time worker
- a 10% cut to eligible student loan balances, with balances of $2,000 or less written off

What is Labour's plan for health?
Labour's plan for affordable healthcare will make it easier to get the care you need, when you need it, from the GP clinic to the emergency department. It includes:

- three free GP visits a year for every New Zealander through a new Medicard, plus free cervical screening for ages 25 to 69 from 1 October 2027 and free maternity scans from July 2028
- free prescriptions from 1 July 2027
- the ED Recovery Plan, with more GP appointments, more nurses and faster emergency care
- the Family Doctor Loan Scheme, with up to 50 loans a year from 1 July 2027 to help doctors buy into owner-operated practices
- the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee

What is Labour doing to create more jobs?
Labour's good jobs plan will back more Kiwis into secure, well-paying jobs so you can build a future here at home. It includes:

- Apprenticeship Boost, with extended employer payments, a $1,000 toolbox grant and five new trades
- Start Work Now, building social housing, improving more than 2,000 schools, clearing the hospital repair backlog and supporting nearly 30,000 apprentices
- Backing Māori into Skilled Work, investing $21 million a year in Māori-led training
- the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee
- the Small Business Action Plan and Small Business First, including a target for 15% of government contracts to go to New Zealand small businesses and start-ups
- Backing Māori Businesses, with an initial target of 5% of government procurement contracts for Māori businesses
- Fairer Workplaces, including restoring pay equity legislation and bringing back Fair Pay Agreements

What else has Labour announced?
Labour has also announced:

- Fairer Workplaces: restoring pay equity legislation, Fair Pay Agreements, the Living Wage across the public service and stronger health and safety law
- Foreign Affairs: recognising the State of Palestine, backing multilateral institutions and international law, and deepening ties with the EU, Canada, ASEAN and the Pacific
- Immigration: planning immigration around New Zealand's capacity, protecting migrants from exploitation and expanding visa-waiver access for Pacific whānau
- A Government You Can Trust: making it easier to vote, harder to buy influence and harder to rush laws through
- Retirement Villages: requiring villages to repay residents within three months
- Crown Guarantee for Community Housing: a $950 million guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency
- Disability: ending annual benefit renewals for people with verified permanent disabilities, and requiring at least 25% of new Kāinga Ora builds to be accessible
- Early Childhood Education: affirming Te Whāriki, working towards pay parity for ECE teachers and stronger oversight
- Fixing the Emissions Trading Scheme: a genuine price on emissions and staying committed to the Paris Agreement
- Backing Māori Businesses: reinstating Progressive Procurement

What is Labour's Fiscal Plan?
Labour's Fiscal Plan sets out how a Labour Government will manage the country's finances:

- return to an OBEGAL surplus by 2028/29
- reduce net debt towards 20% of GDP
- keep core Crown expenditure and revenue at around 33% of GDP
- establish a Parliamentary Budget Office for independent fiscal transparency
- restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate of price stability and maximum sustainable employment
- restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act

How are Labour's policies being funded?
Each policy page sets out its costing and how it is paid for.

Labour's healthcare policies are funded by a simple, targeted 28% capital gains tax on profit from selling commercial or residential investment property, excluding the family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, businesses and inheritances. Every dollar raised is ring-fenced for health, and nine out of 10 New Zealanders will not pay the tax.

Costings include:

- free prescriptions: $74.5 million a year
- free maternity scans: $28.6 million a year
- free cervical screening: $21.6 million a year
- Apprenticeship Boost: an average of $56.5 million a year over four years
- SolarSaver: $160 million over four years
- Backing Māori into Skilled Work: $21 million a year
- the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee: $525 million
- the Small Business Action Plan: $1.56 billion over four years, funded by refocusing Investment Boost
- Start Work Now: around $450 million for schools, $200 million for hospitals and $2.9 billion in capital for housing
- Pay equity is funded within Labour's Fiscal Plan, with future settlements funded through future Budgets as agreements are reached.
- The $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency would only be called on in the unlikely event of a default.

When will Labour's policies start?
- Immediately on taking office: National's hiring freeze ended and winter planning restored (ED Recovery Plan)
- First 100 days of a Labour Government: paid-on-time legislation and payment-time disclosure for small businesses, pay equity legislation restored, Fair Pay Agreements legislation introduced, and the under-16s social media ban legislation
- 1 January 2027: $4 an hour pay rise for care and support workers under Labour's pay equity policy
- 1 April 2027: eligible graduates already repaying their student loan receive a 10% cut; current and future students qualify for the same cut after staying in New Zealand for three years following their study, first qualifying from 2031
- 1 July 2027: $20 fare cap; free prescriptions; Family Doctor Loan Scheme; Apprenticeship Boost expansion (new trades, toolbox grant, mentoring)
- 1 October 2027: free cervical screening (ages 25-69)
- Labour's first Budget in Government in 2027: the $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency
- Within a year of taking office: Start Work Now, with school improvements beginning within 12 to 24 months
- Term 1 2028: new school uniform rules in place and healthy school lunches return
- 1 July 2028: compulsory KiwiSaver employer contributions begin, extended to over-65s; two-year employer payments under Apprenticeship Boost; free maternity scans; Independent Pricing Authority for GP funding
- SolarSaver: EECA support, subsidies and loan schemes up and running within 12 months of taking office
- Backing Māori into Skilled Work: running as soon as possible after Budget 2027
- Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee: applies to graduates from July 2026, with roles offered at graduation from 2027
- Capital gains tax: applies only to profits made after 1 July 2027, and only when the property is sold
- Fiscal Plan: return to an OBEGAL surplus by 2028/29

Who will benefit from Labour's policies?
- Households and shoppers: the fare cap benefits anyone who uses public buses, trains or some ferries; the fuel tax freeze benefits drivers, families, farmers, truck drivers, tradies and businesses; banning price gouging and Fairer Grocery Prices benefit every household buying essentials, independent grocers, food producers and suppliers; A Fair Go For Families benefits anyone buying a car, whiteware, phone or internet plan, subscription, event tickets or gym membership; A Fair Go For Drivers benefits drivers, independent petrol station owners and local mechanics; Banking for Everyone benefits bank customers, small businesses seeking finance and Kiwi fintech businesses; A Better Deal When You Fly benefits air travellers, regional communities and smaller Kiwi airlines; Cutting Back-to-School Costs benefits parents and caregivers, school students and rural families; Cutting Student Debt benefits Kiwis with student debt; SolarSaver benefits homeowners, renters and people without panels in neighbourhoods with a community battery
- Health: the Medicard and its free visits, prescriptions, maternity scans and cervical screening benefit every New Zealander entitled to public healthcare; the ED Recovery Plan benefits patients and families needing GP or emergency care, hospital doctors and nurses, paramedics and older people recovering at home; the Family Doctor Loan Scheme benefits communities with limited GP access; the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee benefits graduate nurses and the patients they care for
- Work and business: Apprenticeship Boost and Start Work Now benefit employers, apprentices, tradies and communities waiting on homes, schools and hospitals; the Small Business Action Plan and Small Business First benefit New Zealand's roughly 600,000 small businesses; Backing Māori into Skilled Work benefits whānau Māori of all ages seeking skills and secure work; Backing Māori Businesses benefits Māori businesses bidding for government contracts; Pay Equity benefits care and support workers, the large majority of whom are women; Fairer Workplaces benefits workers across the public service and beyond; Strengthening KiwiSaver benefits working New Zealanders saving for retirement or a first home; the Future Fund aims to benefit Kiwi workers and businesses
- Families and communities: Keeping Kids off Screens and Safer Online benefit children and teenagers, parents and caregivers, school and kura communities, older people targeted by scammers and anyone who uses social media; Early Childhood Education benefits children, parents, ECE teachers and Pacific language nests, Puna Reo and Te Kōhanga Reo; Disability benefits disabled people, carers and disabled people's organisations; Retirement Villages benefits residents and their families; the Crown guarantee benefits community housing providers; Immigration benefits migrants and Pacific whānau welcoming loved ones; AI for New Zealand aims to benefit all New Zealanders

documents/prescriptions.md.title: Labour's Free Prescriptions with the Medicard
documents/prescriptions.md.text:
## Free Prescriptions Under Labour

From 1 July 2027, Labour will remove the $5 fee on prescriptions to make them free for every New Zealander who is entitled to free public healthcare.

Key facts
- $5 prescription fee removed for every New Zealander entitled to free public healthcare, at every pharmacy
- Currently, free prescriptions only apply to those aged 14 and under, 65 and over, or with a Community Services Card
- Starts 1 July 2027
- Estimated cost: $74.5 million a year, funded by Labour's targeted capital gains tax
- No forms and no claiming money back
- Sits alongside the Medicard's three free doctor's visits, free cervical screening and free maternity scans

### Why make this universally available?

Last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they'd been prescribed because they couldn't afford it.

When people skip medicines because of cost, small problems can become big ones and cost the health system more in the long run. A recent study in the New Zealand Medical Journal found people who couldn't afford their prescriptions were 34 percent more likely to end up in hospital.

Medicine isn't a luxury - it's basic healthcare and should be there for everyone. Making medicines free keeps people well, keeps them out of hospital, and takes pressure off the whole health system.

### Labour's Medicard plan

The Medicard is Labour's plan to make healthcare more affordable. It gives every New Zealander three free doctor's visits a year, free cervical screening and free maternity scans. Free prescriptions will sit alongside our Medicard.

Frequently asked questions
Who will be entitled to free prescriptions?
Everyone in New Zealand who is entitled to free public healthcare. Currently, free prescriptions are only available to those aged 14 and under, 65 and over, or with a Community Services Card.

Why make this universally available?
- Last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they'd been prescribed because they couldn't afford it.
- When people skip medicines because of cost, small problems can become big ones and cost the health system more in the long run. A recent study in the New Zealand Medical Journal found people who couldn't afford their prescriptions were 34 percent more likely to end up in hospital.
- Medicine isn't a luxury – it's basic healthcare and should be there for everyone. Making medicines free keeps people well, keeps them out of hospital, and takes pressure off the whole health system.

How will this be paid for?
Removing the $5 fee is estimated to cost $74.5 million a year. It will be funded by the revenue from a simple, targeted capital gains tax that only applies to the profit when a commercial or investment property is sold (excluding the family home, farms, businesses, inheritance, and KiwiSaver). Every dollar raised by the CGT is ring-fenced for health.

When do prescriptions become free?
From 1 July 2027, the $5 fee will be removed for every New Zealander entitled to free public healthcare, at every pharmacy.

Three free doctor's visits and free prescriptions.

Money back in your pocket - just the start of how life will get better with Labour.

documents/release-a-fair-go-for-families.title: Release: A fair go for families
documents/release-a-fair-go-for-families.text:
##### Release: A fair go for families

Labour's Fair Go Law will stop companies from heaping on extra fees, trapping people in subscriptions, and pushing unnecessary costs onto New Zealanders.

"This election is about the cost of living, and New Zealanders are being hit by hidden fees they never saw coming. Labour will make sure New Zealanders get a fair go at the checkout," Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

"We've all been there before. The gym membership with surprise fees. The meal kit subscription that's impossible to cancel. The worthless insurance on your new car.

"It's more than just frustrating, it's a real burden on families who are already struggling with the high cost of living. Labour will put a stop to it," Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Ban junk car insurance, like paint insurance and mechanical breakdown cover that excludes almost everything
- Stop the hard sell of extended warranties on electronics and whiteware at the checkout
- Require all mandatory fees, including on ticket sales, to be included in the price upfront
- Make every subscription service and gym membership as easy to cancel as it was to sign up
- Ban unfair exit fees on phone and internet contracts, show the full price upfront, plus excessive notice periods and unclear auto-renewals

"Our rule is simple. Don't make money by tricking hardworking people," Labour Commerce and Consumer Affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said.

"Labour's Fair Go Law will bring in new rules for cars, electronics, phones, subscriptions, ticket sales, and gyms.

"People aren't asking for much. Just tell them the real price upfront and make it as easy to leave a subscription or membership as it was to join.

"And those extended warranties? In many cases, what they cover is already your right under the Consumer Guarantees Act.

"This policy builds on our price gouging ban. Whether it's the price on the shelf or the fees piled on top, too many Kiwis are being ripped off.

"You deserve a fair go. Christopher Luxon is too out of touch to see how hidden fees quickly add up, but Labour will act.

"It's all part of our plan to make life better and more affordable for families. New Zealand can't afford another three years of National. Better starts now," Arena Williams said.

### Release: A fair go for families

By LabourVoices

documents/release-a-fair-go-for-kiwi-dri.title: Release: A fair go for Kiwi drivers
documents/release-a-fair-go-for-kiwi-dri.text:
##### Release: A fair go for Kiwi drivers

Labour will make car repairs cheaper, crack down on unfair fuel prices and bring more competition to the pump, putting drivers back in the driver’s seat.

"This election is about the cost of living. For most Kiwis, a car is a necessity, it's how we get to work, drop the kids at school, and get on with life,” Labour leader Chris Hipkins said.

“But under National, the cost of getting around keeps climbing. Labour will give drivers a fair go, whether they’re buying a car, fixing it or filling it up.

“We’ll crack down on price gouging, freeze fuel tax for three years and make it easier for independent mechanics and petrol stations to compete,” Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

Give drivers the right to repair. Require carmakers to give independent mechanics fair access to the manuals, software, tools and information needed to fix modern cars.

Put fuel prices under the microscope. Require the Commerce Commission to report weekly on fuel prices and whether falling costs are being passed on to drivers.

Crack down on fuel price gouging. Apply Labour’s price gouging law to wholesale and retail fuel, allowing unfair pricing to be investigated and overcharges recovered.

Open up the fuel market. Give independent petrol stations fairer access to fuel supplies and stronger protection against restrictive contracts.

Make more room for competition. Require NZTA to consider making surplus land available for independent unmanned petrol stations and EV chargers.

“Your car belongs to you. You should be able to choose who fixes it,” Labour Commerce and Consumer Affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said.

"A right to repair means the mechanic down the road gets a fair shot at your business. It backs local workshops, supports skilled jobs and apprenticeships, and gives drivers a real choice.

“Currently independent workshops have to turn away work because they can't access the information they need to make repairs - Labour will fix this. Australia already did this in 2022 and has led to independent mechanics there able to repair cars 25% cheaper on average than dealerships.

"And we’re bringing in more competition at the pump too. The Commerce Commission found that fuel prices rise faster than they fall, costing Kiwi drivers around $15 million a year. When we were in government, Labour forced the big fuel companies to publish their wholesale prices and opened the market up to independent stations. Now we're going further.

"Labour's price gouging law will apply to fuel. We're giving the Commerce Commission the powers it needs to report fuel prices every week and make sure that when wholesale fuel costs fall, drivers see it at the pump.

“National is driving up prices – we can't afford another three years of their hidden costs and higher prices. Whether you’re buying your car, fixing it, or filling it up, Labour will make sure Kiwi drivers get a fair go,” Arena Williams said.

Stay in the loop by signing up to our mailing list and following us on Facebook, Instagram, and X.

### Release: A fair go for Kiwi drivers

By LabourVoices

05 October 2026

documents/release-getting-kids-off-scree.text:
##### Release: Getting kids off screens and back to being kids

Labour will make it easier for kids to get off screens and back to being kids, with more affordable after-school activities, healthier boundaries in schools and better support for parents to keep their children safe online.

“Too much of childhood is being spent on screens, while sport, hobbies and other after-school activities are out of reach for too many families,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“Parents are struggling to navigate the risks of the online world, and young people are telling us they want action on harmful content and the impact it’s having on their lives.

“Labour is listening. We want kids to have more opportunities to get out, get active, make friends, and enjoy being kids while making sure they’re safer online.

“Our Kids Off Screens plan will give families more affordable alternatives, help schools set healthier boundaries around screens, and give parents better tools to protect their children online.

“Technology has its place, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of childhood. New Zealand is the best place in the world to raise children, and I want us to keep it that way,” Chris Hipkins said.

Labour's Kids Off Screens policy will focus on three areas:

- Affordable activities: Boost funding for community sports and activity grants to make after-school activities more affordable for families.
- Right screen, right time: Introduce healthier boundaries around screen use for kids, in partnership with experts, schools and young people.
- Back parents to keep kids safe: helping parents make informed choices through accessible online safety tools and supporting schools to use technology safely with an education AI app.

The policy complements Labour's AI Action Plan, which includes reviewing existing laws to strengthen protections against online harm, supporting schools to use artificial intelligence safely, and establishing an independent online regulator.

“Keeping kids safe online isn't about turning back the clock or pretending technology doesn't have a place in our lives. It's about preparing for the future and making sure our schools, laws and protections keep pace with the world our children are growing up in," Labour education spokesperson Ginny Andersen said.

“Building on expert recommendations made to the Government in 2024, Labour will work with educators, health experts, and young people to get the balance right in our schools and kura.

“Kids need to be able to concentrate on learning, build friendships and develop the social skills that will serve them throughout their lives.

“Our children deserve a future where technology works for them, not one where they are left to deal with its risks alone. Labour is ready to take action," Ginny Andersen said.

documents/release-labour-to-accelerate-c.text:
##### Release: Labour to accelerate climate action

A Labour government will fix the broken Emissions Trading Scheme as an urgent priority.

“New Zealand should be showing climate leadership; not going backwards as Christopher Luxon’s Government has done,” said Labour leader Chris Hipkins.

“The ETS is broken. The carbon price is too low to drive meaningful emissions reductions. Under National, climate pollution us the only thing that has got cheaper over the last three years.

“Current ETS rules also make it cheaper to plant exotic forests than to grow food. That doesn’t create jobs or help our economy.

“Labour will ensure the ETS Emissions Trading Scheme actually does what it is supposed to do and maintains a genuine price on emissions. We will restore credibility and certainty to the carbon market, generating revenues that can be invested in affordable energy and resilience.

“We will stop the short-term political tinkering that undermines business confidence and puts us all on the back foot.

“Labour is fully committed to the Paris Agreement and will put New Zealand on course to meet its targets. The Paris Agreement is essential for bringing countries together to address a problem affecting every country, every community and every generation. Walking away from it, as National and its mates are planning to do, would be giving up on our kids’ future and impose huge costs on our economy.

“We can’t afford another three years of National’s inaction on climate,” Chris Hipkins said.

“Labour will urgently review the ETS and move quickly to implement changes informed by this work,” Labour climate spokesperson Dr Deborah Russell said.

The review will:

· identify changes to incentivise genuine emissions reductions rather than relying on offsets,

· reconsider the role of forestry (as per PCE’s recommendation)

· ensure the ETS supports New Zealand’s Paris targets

· develop new rules to prevent whole-farm conversions.

· new forestry registrations in the ETS will be paused while this work is completed (as per PCE’s recommendation)

“New Zealanders deserve a government with a plan - one that understands climate action and economic growth go hand-in-hand.

“Climate change is one of the greatest challenges we face, but it is also one of the greatest opportunities available to New Zealand. We can deliver cleaner and more affordable energy, gives businesses the certainty to invest, and help our farmers to compete in global markets by building on New Zealand’s reputation for world class sustainability.

“Labour is committed to protecting our economy and growing our economy – creating good jobs, bringing down household costs and strengthening our energy security,” Dr Deborah Russell said.

##### Release: Labour to cut student debt

Labour will cut student debt by 10%, helping people pay their loans off sooner, and supporting Kiwis to build a future here in New Zealand.

“If you have a student loan and stay in New Zealand, under Labour you will owe less,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“If you've finished your study, didn’t benefit from Fees Free and are still paying off your loan, you'll get the cut on 1 April 2027. Current and future students will get it after staying in New Zealand for three years once they finish their study. And if you owe $2,000 or less, we'll wipe it off completely.

“Student debt can follow people for years, making it harder to save for a home, start a family or simply get ahead.

“This policy means more money to save for a home, start a family, build a business or just have a bit more breathing space.

“New Zealand invests in education because we believe people’s talent and hard work should strengthen our country. We want to make it easier for our graduates – be it nurses and healthcare workers, electricians, or social workers - to stay and build a future in New Zealand.

“That’s the kind of country Labour wants to build, where hard work opens doors, young people can see a future for themselves, and people don’t have to leave New Zealand to get ahead,” Chris Hipkins said.

“Education should open doors, not leave people carrying debt for decades,” Labour tertiary spokesperson Shanan Halbert said.

“This policy means graduates can move forward sooner – with less debt, more of their income in their pocket and a better chance to build their lives here in New Zealand.

“People have done the hard work to get a qualification. They shouldn’t have to spend years watching their student loan barely move.

“Labour will cut that debt and give people a bit more freedom to get on with their lives,” Shanan Halbert said.

Labour will make it cheaper for New Zealanders to catch the bus or train, by capping weekly fares at just $20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 a week everywhere else in New Zealand.

"Our fare cap is a major cost-of-living commitment designed to put money back into the pockets of commuters, students and families," Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

"Cheaper fares mean more freedom, freedom to get to work, freedom to study, freedom to attend appointments and freedom to spend time with family and friends without worrying about the cost.

"This is real cost-of-living relief. It means cheaper commutes, more money left at the end of the week, and a public transport system that works for everyone,” Chris Hipkins said.

"Public transport should help people get ahead, not become a luxury people get priced out of,” Labour transport spokesperson Tangi Utikere said.

"Families deserve certainty. Under Labour's weekly fare cap, people will know exactly what the maximum cost of getting around will be each week.

"We want people catching buses, trains and ferries more often because that means lower household transport costs, less congestion on our roads and stronger public transport networks.

##### Release: Labour to ensure an immigration system that works for New Zealand

A Labour government will plan immigration around what New Zealand’s workforce, housing and infrastructure can support, and make sure migrants who commit to this country are backed to get ahead.

"Immigration should be planned around what New Zealand needs, and it should be managed in a way that's fair to everyone here and everyone who comes," Labour Immigration spokesperson Phil Twyford said.

“If you choose to build your life here, work here and raise your family here, a Labour government will back you to get ahead.

“Getting immigration right is fundamental to New Zealand’s future. We need an immigration system that attracts the skills and talent our country needs, protects migrants from exploitation, and gives people the confidence to build a future here,” Phil Twyford said.

Labour will:

- Plan immigration around New Zealand’s capacity by setting goals through a Government Policy Statement on immigration that reflects our workforce demographic, housing and infrastructure needs
- Encourage migrants to put down roots by extending the period migrants must live here before becoming eligible for permanent residence from two years to four, supported by a programme of New Zealand orientation and civic education delivered by community education providers to strengthen social cohesion.
- Protect migrants from exploitation by enabling migrants to move between accredited employers after three months, strengthening the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme, and improving access to support in their communities.
- Treat people with decency by protecting humanitarian appeals against deportation, setting up a citizenship pathway for children born in New Zealand, and reviewing parent visa, health, and English-language rules.

“We should be ambitious about the contribution migrants can make to New Zealand, to our communities and to our economy, while making sure our immigration settings work for the country as a whole.

“That means having clear and predictable rules, protecting people from exploitation, and giving those who choose to make New Zealand their home a genuine opportunity to get ahead.

“Migrants bring skills, energy, and enterprise to New Zealand. A Labour government will back people to build their lives and careers here, while ensuring immigration supports the long-term interests of New Zealand,” Phil Twyford said.

documents/release-labour-to-give-kiwis-a.title: Release: Labour to give Kiwis a better deal when you fly
documents/release-labour-to-give-kiwis-a.text:
##### Release: Labour to give Kiwis a better deal when you fly

Labour will give Kiwis clearer prices, stronger passenger rights, and more choice when they fly.

“For many New Zealanders flying is how we get home for a birthday, get to a hospital appointment in another city, or keep a business running,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“But flying is expensive, and on many regional routes there is little or no competition. Kiwis are struggling with the cost of living and are finding it harder and harder to make those important trips. Only Labour has a real plan to tackle it across the economy.

“Labour will make prices more transparent, open opportunities for smaller airlines to compete and give passengers more rights.

“Kiwis deserve better prices, better protection and more choices when they fly,” Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Show the real price up front: Require airlines to show all-in, real-time airfares so Kiwis can properly compare the true cost of flights.
- Put passengers first: Require big airlines to provide automatic refunds when flights are cancelled or significantly changed, with compensation or reimbursement when checked baggage is significantly delayed or paid services aren’t delivered.
- Open the skies to more competition: Require fair access to essential airport infrastructure so smaller airlines can grow and compete.
- Make airlines more accountable: Require airlines to publicly report delays, cancellations and baggage performance, alongside greater scrutiny of fares, costs and profits.
- Keep airport costs under control: Make sure airports can raise capital and borrow cheaply, so essential infrastructure investment doesn’t unnecessarily push up airfares.

“For many regional routes there is limited or no competition. That means fewer choices for travellers and less pressure on airlines to offer better prices and service,” Labour commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said.

“Smaller airlines shouldn’t have to compete with one hand tied behind their backs. Labour will give them fair access to the airport facilities they need to grow and connect regional New Zealand.

“We’ll make airlines more accountable, with greater scrutiny of fares, costs and profits and clear reporting on delays, cancellations and baggage.

“When an airline screws up, passengers shouldn’t have to fight to get their money back. If your flight is cancelled or significantly changed, you’ll get an automatic refund.

“Regional connections matter too. When an essential air service is at risk, Labour will bring the industry together to find long-term solutions to keep communities connected.

“National’s answer has been to hand smaller airlines a bit of extra cash to help them get by, while leaving the barriers to competition in place. That won’t help smaller airlines grow or give passengers more choice.

“Labour will open up competition, give smaller airlines a fair shot and give passengers enforceable rights when airlines let them down,” Arena Williams said.

documents/release-labour-to-make-it-safe.title: Release: Labour to make it safer for Kiwis online
documents/release-labour-to-make-it-safe.text:
##### Release: Labour to make it safer for Kiwis online

Labour will ensure Kiwis have more control over online content, while strengthening protections for our kids.

“Social media is part of everyday life. It helps us stay connected, share ideas and keep in touch with the people we care about,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“But the big technology companies have too much power over our online experience. At the same time, scams are becoming more sophisticated, fake images and videos are harder to spot, and a lot of parents are worried about what their children are seeing.

“Parents shouldn’t have to take on big tech on their own.

“Labour will put basic rules in place for big technology companies, give people more control over their online experience, and strengthen protections against harmful content,” Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Ban social media for under-16s. We’ll get current legislation through its first reading and to select committee within our first 100 days, and add strong privacy safeguards on age checks.
- Give you more control of your feed. Everyone will be able to choose between an algorithm-driven feed, or posts only from accounts they follow, and be able to switch back at any time.
- Make platforms responsible for safety. We’ll introduce a new “Digital Duty of Care” law that will require platforms to identify risks and protect Kiwis from harmful content and addictive designs.
- Set up an independent online regulator with the power to fine platforms that break the rules.

“The algorithms deciding what we see are designed to keeping us scrolling, but that’s not always what Kiwis want,” Labour science, technology and innovation spokesperson Reuben Davidson said.

“You might like your recommended feed, and that’s fine, but you should have the choice to switch to seeing only posts from people and accounts you follow.

“Labour will get legislation on the under-16 social media ban moving in our first 100 days, and we’ll make it stronger at select committee with new privacy protections too.

“We’ll join Australia in introducing a new ‘Digital Duty of Care’ law, putting the responsibility of stopping online harm – like bullying, content promoting eating disorders or self-harm, and deepfakes – more on big tech.

“And to enforce these new laws, we will establish an independent online regulator to make sure platforms meet their responsibilities.

“The internet should be a place where people can connect, learn and enjoy themselves.

“New Zealanders have seen the very real harms that occur online, the platforms have had their chance to address it, but they’ve failed to act. It's time for real action to protect young people online.

"Labour is committed to taking that immediate action” Reuben Davidson said.

##### Release: Labour will back Kiwis and grow the economy

Labour will grow the economy, get the books back into surplus and make sure hard-working New Zealanders can get ahead.

"New Zealand should be a country where hard work gets you somewhere. Where you can get ahead, put down roots and know your kids will have opportunities here," Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

"National came in promising to fix the economy. Instead, unemployment is up, businesses are struggling and everything costs more.

"Labour will get the books back into shape but we won’t do it by making life harder for New Zealanders or cutting the services they reply on. You can’t cut your way to growth.

"We’ll invest in the things that make New Zealand stronger – our hospitals and schools, infrastructure, skills and the businesses that create jobs.

"New Zealand has enormous potential. Our job is to back the people and businesses that can realise it, while leaving the country stronger for the next generation," Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Balance the books and return to surplus. Return to original measure of OBEGAL, achieve surplus by 2029/30 and maintain a sustainable fiscal position over the forecast period.

- Bring down debt. We will aim to reduce net debt down to 20% of GDP over time and prioritise investments which support a strong growing economy.

- Keep government spending and revenue sustainable. Core Crown Expenditure and revenue will be maintained at around 33% of GDP when the CGT is fully implemented.

- Strengthen scrutiny of Government spending by establishing an independent Parliamentary Budget Office to analyse Government finances and election commitments.

- Restore the Reserve Bank dual mandate to consider price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

"Labour will be responsible with taxpayers’ money, balancing the books and bringing down debt, while giving New Zealand the capacity to invest in its future," Labour finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said.

"Labour will return the books to surplus by 2029/30 and reduce net debt over time but we won't do that by cutting the foundations of our economy.

“Under National unemployment is at an 11-year high, business liquidations are up 71%, homelessness and KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are at record levels, and public services are under pressure. That isn’t economic success.

"Strong public services are an investment in New Zealand’s future. Labour will make every dollar count, invest where it matters and back the people and businesses that can grow our economy," Barbara Edmonds said.

##### Release: Labour will make price gouging illegal

Labour will crack down on companies who charge New Zealanders excessive prices for essential goods and services.

"New Zealanders are working hard, but they’re still going backwards. Christopher Luxon promised he’d fix the cost of living, but he’s just made it worse, all while a handful of big companies price gouge households - charging whatever they like for the things families can't do without," Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

"Right now, a company big enough to dodge competition can charge excessive prices for the basics, like food and fuel, and there's no law against it. Labour will change that, by making it illegal for big powerful companies to rip off New Zealanders on the essentials," Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Make it illegal for big companies with substantial market power to charge excessive prices for essential goods and services, or to pay unfairly low prices to suppliers.
- Set a clear legal test for the first time: prices well above what they would otherwise be in a competitive market, sustained over time.
- Give the Commerce Commission the power to investigate price gouging and back groups representing consumers and suppliers to do the same
- Require companies that gouge to pay penalties and hand back every dollar of excess profit.

“Nearly one in three New Zealand households couldn't afford enough food last year. Since National took office, the price of butter has gone up 58 percent, bread is up 45 percent, and mince is up 30 percent,” Labour Commerce and Consumer Affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said.

“Meanwhile, the growers who put food on our shelves get squeezed by the big players just as hard as the families buying it.

"Labour’s policy will ensure that companies with significant market power are charging a fair price for the things that your family can't do without.

“This is aimed at a small number of very large companies, it won't touch the 97 percent of New Zealand businesses that are small, like your local dairy or cafe.

“It also only applies in markets for essentials, like food, power, fuel, transport, telecommunications banking, and insurance.

"Rules like these already operate in the United Kingdom, Europe, Canada, and Australia. It's time New Zealanders had the same protection.

“Christopher Luxon is too out of touch to realise that families can’t even afford the basics under his policies. Households are working harder just to keep up, while the biggest companies post record profits off excessive prices.

“A Labour Government will work to make your life easier and more affordable. This election is about the cost of living and New Zealanders can't afford another three years of National," Arena Williams said.

Labour will make KiwiSaver work harder for more New Zealanders, helping Kiwis save, build wealth and retire with security.

"Labour is the party of KiwiSaver. We believe every New Zealander should have the opportunity to build a secure future," Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

"Sir Michael Cullen turned that belief into KiwiSaver, while National voted against it. Today KiwiSaver funds exceed $138 billion and are an important source of investment in our economy.

"Under National too many New Zealanders are struggling to pay the bills, let alone save for tomorrow. More than a million working-age KiwiSaver members aren’t contributing at all, while 83,400 are on a savings suspension.

“New Zealanders cannot afford another three years of going backwards. Labour will get our economy growing again so working people can build something for their future.

"KiwiSaver is one of Labour’s proudest legacies. We created it, and now we’re going to make it work better for people," Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Make employer contributions compulsory, and lift to 6 percent by 2032, including when employees reduce or pause their own contributions.
- Set the employee default at 4 percent, remove the minimum contribution rate, and give employees more flexibility to choose their rate as circumstances change.
- Ban new total remuneration contracts that absorb employer KiwiSaver contributions into salaries.
- Extend employer contributions to workers over 65.
- Keep KiwiSaver growing for parents while they’re on paid parental leave.
- Explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders.

"Labour built KiwiSaver and changed the way New Zealanders save. Now we want it to work harder for more people," Labour finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said.

"National has made it harder for Kiwis to save and now wants to force workers to put more in. Labour will require employers to contribute at the same amount as National is proposing but give workers more flexibility when money is tight.

“We’ll also make KiwiSaver fairer for parents, older Kiwis and broaden who benefits – working with self-employed New Zealanders on more flexible ways to build their savings in the scheme.

“From 1 July 2028, employer contributions will become compulsory and will extend to paid parental leave and workers over 65. We’ll phase changes across our KiwiSaver policy carefully, giving workers and businesses certainty.

"Stronger KiwiSaver means more wealth in Kiwi hands and more investment here at home. Labour will back Kiwis to save and back the businesses that will grow our economy," Barbara Edmonds said.

“Only Labour will act decisively. We will open the market so more supermarkets can offer lower prices, giving shoppers more choice and a better deal at the checkout.

##### Release: Labour's plan to bring down costs for Kiwis

Labour has released its Cost of Living Action Plan, with help for families on food bills, healthcare costs, petrol, transport, and the cost of getting kids to school.

“Everywhere I go I hear the same thing: people are working hard, but they’re still finding less left at the end of each week. That's why getting the cost of living under control is Labour’s number one priority,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“The weekly groceries. Seeing a doctor. Power bills. Petrol. It all adds up. Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living, but under National things have gotten worse. New Zealand can’t afford another three years of National making life harder and more expensive.

“Labour has a plan. We’ll help with the bills you face every week, and we’ll crack down on big companies ripping you off, so you get a fairer deal.

“Getting costs under control is also about making sure people have enough money coming in, which is why our plan is about good jobs too. We’ll back apprentices and tradies, and get work started fixing our schools and hospitals,” Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Give every New Zealander three free GP visits a year with a new Medicard
- Cap public transport fares at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 everywhere else
- Freeze the fuel tax for three years
- Help households install solar, with low-interest SolarSaver loans
- Make price gouging on essentials illegal, and make companies pay back what they’ve overcharged
- Scrap the $5 prescription charge
- Crack down on hidden fees, subscription traps and junk insurance
- Give smaller Kiwi businesses, from independent mechanics to local grocers, a fair shot against the big players
- Cut student debt by 10%, and back 30,000 apprentices into work
- Bring back fresh, locally made school lunches, and work to restore rural school buses

“Three free doctors visits could save a couple up to $500 a year. A daily bus commuter could save around $25 a week. And a family with solar could cut around $1,000 a year off their power bill,” Chris Hipkins said.

“These are real savings for real people. And every promise we’ve made is fully costed and paid for in our fiscal plan.

“Today, I am also announcing two new commitments to help parents with household costs. Labour will bring back fresh, locally-made school lunches, and we will work to restore the rural school bus routes that National cut.

“As a parent myself, I know how school costs add up. Labour’s school lunches will mean one less meal to find money for and a healthy lunch for your children. It also means more jobs in your local community.

“And bringing back rural school buses that National cancelled will save parents on petrol costs, not to mention time and stress.

“Kiwis should be able to put food on the table, see a doctor and get where they need to go, with something left over at the end of the week. Your hard work should get you somewhere.

“Lower bills. Good jobs. A fairer deal. That’s Labour’s plan,” Chris Hipkins said.

##### Release: Move on Bill still punishes the homeless

How can that be our response to a seeing a child live on the street?” Labour justice spokesperson Camilla Belich said.

“But the fundamental problem remains. Criminalising people for sleeping rough when they have no other option is wrong, and it shows just how out of touch Christopher Luxon is.

“The Bill does nothing to address the underlying problem of homelessness. National stopped Kāinga Ora from making more homes available, stopped people in need from accessing emergency housing, and made the cost of living worse.

"New Zealanders have made it very clear this Bill is not the solution to our housing crisis that National made worse. We simply can't afford three more years of National treating people as problems to be swept under the rug," Camilla Belich said.

documents/rnz-chris-hipkins-promises-to-.text:

## Chris Hipkins promises to reverse pay equity changes in first 100 days if elected

Anna Sargent

Caption:Chris Hipkins meets a member of the public at a community meeting in Spreydon.Photo credit:RNZ / Anna Sargent

Chris Hipkins has made a campaign commitment to reverse pay equity changes in the first 100 days of a Labour government, during a packed public meeting in Christchurch.

The Labour leader received a standing ovation walking into a community hall in Spreydon on Monday night where close to 200 people filled the room, with some spilling out the doors.

The meeting was held a day after Labour launched its campaign, promising "plenty more fire" this election.

Hipkins received a warm reception, and many of his answers were met with applause.

"It's great to see the energy that is going to propel our campaign to victory," he told the room.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins spoke to a packed public meeting in Spreydon on Monday 28 September, 2026.

RNZ / Anna Sargent

One of the biggest cheers of the night came after a question by a support worker on Labour's stance on restoring pay equity.

Hipkins said Labour would quickly reverse pay equity law changes if elected.

"I think probably the most reprehensible thing I have seen in my time as a member of Parliament was the government's decision last year with no notice, with no warning, with no consultation, to pass under urgency a law that cancelled pay equity for tens of thousands of women," Hipkins said.

"I want to give you a reassurance that within the first 100 days we are back in government we will reverse that change.

"When we have reversed that change, care and support workers will be the first in the queue to sit down with to get a settlement because you've waited long enough."

Hipkins was asked by a 13-year-old girl what was the most important thing his government would do to support women and girls in New Zealand, to which he said "restoring pay equity".

Hipkins received a warm reception, and many of his answers were met with applause.

RNZ / Anna Sargent

Hipkins said this election was a cost-of-living election and repeated the line to the crowd that the country "cannot afford three more years of this government".

He promoted Labour's policies including the SolarSaver programme, the apprenticeship boost and cutting student loan debt.

For about an hour the crowd asked a gamut of questions, touching on healthcare, housing, pay equity, AI and local government.

Attendees RNZ spoke to after the meeting were impressed by Hipkins.

A nurse at Christchurch Hospital, who did not wish to be named, said Hipkins had given him hope.

"It's nice to have a future prime minister who is human. We've got a prime minister at the moment where the two tails are wagging the dog. We've got a leader here," he said.

One woman said there was not a single thing said she disagreed with.

"This is the first time I've felt hope for a long time. I think his integrity and what the Labour Party is trying to do for every Kiwi came through," she said.

Hipkins has promised to explain how Labour's promises will be paid for after the government opens its books on Tuesday, after which the party will need to crunch the numbers.

documents/rnz-labour-commits-to-securing.title: Labour commits to securing first pay equity deal by next Budget | RNZ
documents/rnz-labour-commits-to-securing.text:
29 September 2026, 6:51pm

## Labour commits to securing first pay equity deal by next Budget

Russell Palmer

Photo credit:RNZ / Nick Monro

While the government is hailing a bigger surplus as evidence its plan is working, not all the numbers are so rosy and the opposition is warning of more cuts to come.

Both major parties will have explaining to do, with spending cuts built into the projections and Labour yet to explain how it will pay for its promises.

The party's Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds has also added to leader Chris Hipkins' commitment to pass pay equity legislation within 100 days of being elected, promising the first deal - with care and support workers - would be done by her first Budget.

The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (Prefu) opened the government's books for the first time since the Budget in May and revealed improved numbers.

However, economists and business groups have warned the improvements mask some deeper challenges.

#### Labour promises pay equity deal done by first Budget

Edmonds pledged the first pay equity deal under the restored legislation would be done by the time of her first Budget.

"That's my commitment," she said.

"I want to be able to settle this by my first Budget for that care and support workers deal, especially because that's what the unions are saying should be done first.

"We might have to do a mini-Budget anyway because of just the other commitments that we might have, but obviously we'll probably have to set up a contingency for it given there is none."

She refused to accept that could impact the government's ability to negotiate.

"No. What's hamstringing is that our working women have less pay in their pocket over the last three years."

She fended off repeated questions about how much the party would set aside for restoring pay equity deals under the previous settings, saying her fiscal plan setting out the contingency funding would be coming "very soon" and the figure would be "sufficient".

RNZ / Nick Monro

Hipkins, speaking in Auckland after a speech to the EMA, said the Prefu was "the verdict" on National's track record with government debt, unemployment, and inflation staying higher for longer, and a return to surplus still forecast later than the update prior to the last election.

Both stood by the modelling for their capital gains tax in spite of weaker house price growth, saying revenue was still expected to be higher than when Labour did the costings.

"We deliberately costed it conservatively," Hipkins said.

#### 'Our plan is working' - National

National leader Christopher Luxon was touting the improved numbers, but also appeared to back off earlier commitments to changing the superannuation eligibility age.

He praised Finance Minister Nicola Willis' "responsible economic management".

"Our plan is genuinely working, it is working. We have been doing the right things from day one, under Nicola's leadership. She's done an exceptionally good job, there is no better finance minister in this country, and she's going to go down as one of the greatest."

However, having previously said the party would campaign on raising the age from 65 at this year's election, he cast doubt on National's ability to secure changes to the superannuation age of eligibility.

Christopher Luxon speaks to media at The Borough Cafe in Tawa on 29 September 2026.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"If we do it, it would need to be in a very slow, considered, you know, giving people lots of advance notice and lots of time, but it also does require a degree of political consensus as well, and that's missing at the moment," he said.

Willis at this year's Budget railed against parties refusing to lift the age, saying they were "prepared to rob everyone in this country under the age of 50 for their own political expediency".

#### 'Hope is this government's plan' - Greens

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick brought back the prime minister's quote that "hope is not a plan" from the beginning of the fuel crisis, levelling it at the coalition.

"Unfortunately today it appears as though hope is this government's plan, as they sit on their hands and refuse to do anything to actually increase our resilience and improve New Zealanders' outlook," she told reporters.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Swarbrick pointed to what she said was a missed opportunity for the government to decarbonise the economy and better prepare the country for price shocks when the Strait of Hormuz initially closed.

The Luxon government had driven fuel inflation higher, she said, pointing at 10 additional risks highlighted by Treasury in the Prefu - particularly $5b in committed but unfunded military spending.

The government had "very clearly" shifted the cost of the economic recovery to New Zealand, she said.

#### 'Vindicated' - Seymour

In Auckland, ACT leader David Seymour said the Prefu had "vindicated" his party's drive for savings.

"We have saved money in this government, but actually nowhere near enough. And as the bond market increases interest rates on government debt all around the world, we are going to have to go further and faster to balance the books with no new taxes."

He reiterated his call for fewer government departments, and reducing the number of public servants to 1 percent of the total population.

"The surplus being promised is two years later than was promised before the last election. To achieve that is going to require major reductions in the number of public servants and government departments, which I think we should do."

RNZ / Nick Monro

He said that could be achieved without affecting nurses, police officers or doctors, and also reiterated his call for fuel taxes to continue rising.

"You've got to collect enough money from your excise tax to pay for the roads. If you're not prepared to do that, you're not being honest."

#### Too early for tax cuts - economist

Independent economist Cameron Bagrie told Checkpoint that after repeated delays on reaching surplus, the Prefu was one of the first reports showing the goalposts a bit closer.

Audio player for "Bigger surplus forecast in pre-election fiscal update" removed for printing

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics/1653587%2Flabour-commits-to-securing-first-pay-equity-deal-by-next-budget

### Bigger surplus forecast in pre-election fiscal update

Checkpoint

But it all relied on the government making further spending cuts of 2.5 percentage points over four to five years.

"If you strip out New Zealand superannuation and if you strip out interest costs which are going to go up as a share of GDP, then the belt tightening is 2.9 percent of GDP," he said.

With spending on health, defence and education expected to rise as a percentage of GDP, the cuts would have to come from core services, law and order, cultural services or superannuation, he said.

"Yeah... she's running pretty skinny over the next sort of few years."

Willis had at a recent Business NZ conference hinted National might campaign on more income tax cuts, but Bagrie said that should wait.

"Not at the moment ... once we get a little bit of money in the tin, hopefully, yeah, we should be able to tax adjust tax brackets and remove what's called the effect of fiscal drag. But that's tomorrow's story, it's not today's."

He said the jobs data shows the economic recovery is being skewed towards the owners of capital, rather than workers.
