## Start Work Now

What we'll deliver How we'll do it Why the work cannot wait Funding FAQs
Labour will build the homes, improve the schools and repair the hospitals our communities need - creating good jobs, supporting local businesses, and getting Kiwis back on the tools.

Key facts
- More than 2,000 schools will receive funding to improve buildings and grounds
- Health New Zealand's hospital repair backlog will be cleared - only 18 of 152 projects were finished as of 31 March 2026
- Kāinga Ora will get building again plus reliable funding for community housing providers
- Nearly 30,000 apprentices will receive $1,000 towards tools and gear to get started
- Fully funded and ready to start within a year of taking office

This election is about the cost of living. The cost of living is not only about what you pay at the checkout or when you fill up the car. It is also about whether you have a good job and enough money coming in to cover the bills.

That is why good jobs are at the heart of Labour's plan to address the cost of living.

National promised to fix the cost of living. It hasn't. Everything costs more, unemployment has gone up, and well-paid, secure work has become harder to find. Another three years of National means more cuts, fewer jobs and higher prices.

New Zealanders deserve a fair shot: secure work, decent public services and the chance to build a good life close to family.

But right now, 171,000 New Zealanders are out of work. Since National took office, 20,000 people have lost their jobs in construction. Unemployment is now at an 11-year high. Building firms are struggling and skilled Kiwis are leaving the country.

At the same time, homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing.

Labour will bring those things together. We will get people back on the tools by getting on with the work New Zealand needs. We will also expand Apprenticeship Boost and introduce Māori Trades Training to train more people for skilled jobs in the trades.

We'll create jobs by starting work that has been put off for too long. This is practical work that communities need: building homes, improving classrooms and repairing hospitals.

National has put work on hold while unemployment has gone up. Labour will start the work now.

### What Labour will deliver

#### Better schools

Improvements at more than 2,000 state and integrated schools, with work for local firms in towns and cities across New Zealand.

#### Better hospitals

Long-overdue repairs so hospital buildings are safe, reliable and fit for patients and staff.

#### More social housing

More secure homes for families and more work for builders, electricians, plumbers, engineers and apprentices.

#### More work for local businesses

Useful projects that help local businesses and tradies and create jobs.

#### Back more people to learn a trade

Support more tradies into work and to gain a qualification, so they can earn more.

### How we'll do it

A Labour Government will get essential building and repair work under way quickly. We will focus on the work that needs doing now, not make big promises that take years to start.

#### Homes

- Build more social housing. We'll get Kāinga Ora building again.
- Back community housing providers. We'll provide reliable funding so community providers can plan ahead, alongside a government guarantee that reduces borrowing costs and helps funding go further.

#### Schools

Improve schools across New Zealand. We will provide nearly every school with funding to improve its buildings and grounds, creating work for local builders, electricians, plumbers and other tradespeople.

Schools will be able to improve classrooms, heating, plumbing, drainage, playgrounds and sports facilities. The work will begin in 12 to 24 months, getting people into work quickly.

#### Hospitals

- Clear the hospital repair backlog. We will direct Health New Zealand to finish the remediation projects already on its books.
- Keep hospitals safe and reliable. Once that work is completed, Labour will invest to fix more hospital buildings and essential systems.

#### Apprenticeships

Train the next generation. Apprenticeship Boost and Māori Trades Training will back local businesses to take people on and train them.

Labour will support nearly 30,000 apprentices and provide $1,000 towards the tools and equipment they need to get started.

### National isn't working

Unemployment is at an 11-year high. Under National, 20,000 construction workers have lost their jobs.

National has cancelled, paused and delayed work. Good firms have lost contracts. Tradespeople have lost hours. Young New Zealanders are wondering whether they have a better future in Australia.

But the work that needs doing has not gone away. Delaying it only makes the problems worse and the eventual bill bigger.

We need to stop delaying the work and get on with it.

### Why the work cannot wait

This work is also part of Labour's plan to address the cost of living. It will create good jobs and reliable incomes now, while fixing problems before they become more expensive.

New Zealand needs more homes. Building them gives families security and puts people to work in every part of the country.

A third of school buildings are more than 50 years old. Schools have classrooms, heating, plumbing, playgrounds and other facilities that need attention now.

Health New Zealand looks after about 1,200 buildings with an average age of 47 years. But it spends only around half as much on upkeep as comparable organisations.

At 31 March 2026, only 18 of 152 hospital repair projects had been finished. Another 55 had not moved beyond the early planning stage.

Delaying this work can hit New Zealanders twice. It means fewer jobs and less money coming into households now, followed by a bigger repair bill later.

Putting the work off does not save money. It costs more later and leaves communities with buildings that are not good enough.

### Good work builds strong communities

When a local building firm wins a contract, the benefit spreads.

Tradies get hours. Suppliers receive orders. Apprentices learn a trade. People can cover their bills with a little left over to spend in local shops and businesses.

That is what a good government should do: invest public money carefully, support decent work and leave communities stronger.

Labour will back local firms, give apprentices a start and create good jobs in the communities that need them.

### Fully funded, ready to start in a year

Labour has funded this plan and will use proven ways of getting the work under way. This plan will be funded from future operating and capital allowances.

#### Education package

We will allocate around $450 million to improve the physical environment of New Zealand schools, made up of around $400 million in capital funding for state schools and around $50 million in operating funding for the proprietors of integrated schools, allocated on a similar basis.

#### Health package

We will allocate $200 million in capital for the National Remediation Programme and the Small-Scale Remediation projects.

#### Housing package

We will allocate $2.9 billion of capital for Kāinga Ora to build more state houses. It also allocates $760 million in operating funding to cover the additional Income-Related Rent Subsidy and operating costs for Kāinga Ora and Community Housing Providers.

Labour will invest and get on with the job.

Frequently asked questions
What will Labour build under this policy?
Labour will build more social housing through Kāinga Ora, improve more than 2,000 state and integrated schools, clear the hospital repair backlog, and support nearly 30,000 apprentices into the trades.

How many jobs and apprentices will this create?
Labour will support nearly 30,000 apprentices and provide $1,000 towards the tools and gear they need to get started, alongside creating construction and trades work for local builders, electricians, plumbers, engineers and other tradespeople across housing, schools and hospitals.

What will happen to schools under this policy?
Nearly every school will receive funding to improve its buildings and grounds, including classrooms, heating, plumbing, drainage, playgrounds and sports facilities. Work will begin within 12 to 24 months, and more than 2,000 state and integrated schools will benefit.

What will happen to hospitals under this policy?
Labour will direct Health New Zealand to finish the remediation projects already on its books, clearing the existing repair backlog. Once that work is completed, Labour will invest to fix more hospital buildings and essential systems.

What will happen to housing under this policy?
Labour will get Kāinga Ora building social housing again, and provide reliable, guaranteed funding for community housing providers so they can plan ahead and reduce their borrowing costs.

How much will this cost and how is it funded?
The plan is funded from future operating and capital allowances.

For the education package, we will allocate $450 million to improve the physical environment of New Zealand schools, made up of $400 million in capital funding for state schools and around $50 million in operating funding for the proprietors of integrated schools, allocated on a similar basis.

When will the work start?
Within one year of taking office.

Why does Labour say this work can't wait?
A third of school buildings are more than 50 years old.

Health New Zealand looks after around 1,200 buildings with an average age of 47 years but spends only around half as much on upkeep as comparable organisations. At 31 March 2026, only 18 of 152 hospital repair projects had been finished, and 55 had not moved beyond early planning.

Delaying this work costs more later and leaves communities with buildings that aren't good enough, while also meaning fewer jobs now.

Build homes. Fix schools. Repair hospitals. Get Kiwis back on the tools.

Better starts now.

## Strengthening KiwiSaver for the Future

A better future How it works Fiscal impact FAQs
Labour will create more jobs and strengthen KiwiSaver, so New Zealanders can earn more, save more, and enjoy the retirement they've worked so hard for.

Key facts
- Employer contributions become compulsory from 1 July 2028, including when an employee reduces or pauses their own contributions
- Compulsory employer contributions rise to 6% by 2032
- Employee default contribution set at 4%, with the minimum contribution rate removed for more flexibility
- Bans new total remuneration contracts that absorb employer KiwiSaver contributions into salaries
- A new KiwiSaver contribution for parents while on paid parental leave
- Employer contributions extended to people working beyond 65, from 1 July 2028
- Labour will explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders

If you work hard, you should be able to get ahead and build a secure future. That's why Labour created KiwiSaver.

KiwiSaver is now helping millions of New Zealanders buy their first home, build a nest egg, and plan for retirement with greater security. KiwiSaver is now worth more than $138 billion and is an important source of investment for New Zealand businesses.

Labour built KiwiSaver, and a Labour Government will strengthen it.

National can't be trusted with New Zealanders' savings. A National Government cut the KiwiSaver government contribution in 2011 and again in 2025, and scrapped the $1,000 kick-start in 2015. New Zealanders can't risk another three years of National.

A Labour Government will strengthen KiwiSaver for the next generation. We will back people to save more throughout their working lives, while making sure they have flexibility when money is tight.

### A better future

Your hard work should pay off, not just in your pay packet and weekly budget, but in the savings you build over your lifetime.

With costs going up, too many New Zealanders are struggling to save for the future. More than a million working-age members aren't contributing to their KiwiSaver, and 83,400 people have had to pause their savings, allowing their employers to stop contributing too and leaving them further behind.

When people can't save, it means they have less financial security, fewer choices, and a tougher retirement. Getting through a tough patch shouldn't stop you from saving for the future. Labour will fix this.

A stronger KiwiSaver will help more New Zealanders:

- Keep saving when household budgets are under pressure
- Build a deposit for their first home
- Plan for the future
- Retire with more security

### How it works

Labour is announcing practical measures to help New Zealanders save for the future. Labour will:

- Make employer contributions compulsory from 1 July 2028, and lift them to 6% by 2032, including when employees reduce or pause their own contributions
- Set the employee default at 4%, remove the minimum contribution rate, and give people more flexibility to adjust their contributions as circumstances change
- Ban new total remuneration contracts that absorb employer KiwiSaver contributions into salaries
- Provide a KiwiSaver contribution for parents while they're on paid parental leave
- Extend employer contributions to people working beyond the age of 65 years from 1 July 2028
- Explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders

Under a Labour Government, by 2032 most working New Zealanders will have more going into KiwiSaver, helping them plan for the future, buy a first home and retire with greater security. When money is tight, they will also be able to reduce their own contributions without missing out on their employer's contribution.

### Building on KiwiSaver's legacy

KiwiSaver is one of Labour's proudest achievements. When Sir Michael Cullen created it, National voted against it.

Today, KiwiSaver is part of the fabric of New Zealand. It helps people buy their first home and prepare for retirement, while providing a source of investment for New Zealand businesses.

But it doesn't work well for everyone. It works best for people with steady employment who can afford regular contributions.

Only 44% of self-employed people actively contribute to KiwiSaver, compared with 78% of employees. People working beyond 65 can miss out on employer contributions, while most parents on paid parental leave stop contributing to their KiwiSaver. Labour will make KiwiSaver work for more New Zealanders.

### Fiscal impact

Making the employer contribution compulsory and increasing the employer contribution to 6% over time will affect revenue from the Employer Superannuation Contribution Tax (ESCT). This will help fund government contributions to paid parental leave recipients and meet the government's higher costs as an employer, which will be managed through the Budget process.

### Investing in our future

A stronger KiwiSaver means more wealth in Kiwi hands, and more capital invested in our economy.

It will help people plan for the future while backing businesses, creating good jobs and growing our economy.

Labour will phase in these changes carefully, giving people and businesses certainty.

Frequently asked questions
When does compulsory employer contribution start, and how high does it go?
Employer contributions become compulsory from 1 July 2028, including when an employee reduces or pauses their own contributions, and will lift to 6% by 2032.

What is the new employee default contribution rate?
Labour will set the employee default contribution at 4% and remove the minimum contribution rate, giving people more flexibility to adjust their own contributions as their circumstances change.

What are total remuneration contracts, and why is Labour banning new ones?
Total remuneration contracts absorb an employer's KiwiSaver contribution into an employee's overall salary package, rather than paying it on top. Labour will ban new total remuneration contracts of this kind, so employer KiwiSaver contributions are paid in addition to salary.

Will parents get a KiwiSaver contribution while on paid parental leave?
Yes. Labour will provide a KiwiSaver contribution for parents while they are on paid parental leave. Most parents on paid parental leave currently stop contributing to their KiwiSaver.

What changes for people working past the age of 65?
From 1 July 2028, Labour will extend employer contributions to people working beyond the age of 65, who currently can miss out on employer KiwiSaver contributions.

What about self-employed people?
Only 44% of self-employed people actively contribute to KiwiSaver, compared with 78% of employees. Labour will explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders.

Why is Labour doing this?
Labour created KiwiSaver, which is now worth more than $138 billion and helps New Zealanders buy their first home and save for retirement. National cut the KiwiSaver government contribution in 2011 and again in 2025, and scrapped the $1,000 kick-start in 2015. More than a million working-age members are not currently contributing to KiwiSaver, and 83,400 people have had to pause their savings, which also pauses their employer's contribution. A stronger KiwiSaver will help more New Zealanders keep saving under pressure, build a deposit, and retire with more security.

What is the fiscal impact of these changes?
Making the employer contribution compulsory and increasing it to 6% over time affects revenue from the Employer Superannuation Contribution Tax (ESCT), and will help fund the new government contribution for people on paid parental leave and the government's higher costs as an employer. This will be managed through the Budget process, with changes phased in from 2027/28 to 2030/31.

Backing Kiwis to save and backing the businesses that will grow our economy.

Labour built KiwiSaver and a Labour Government will strengthen it.
